The greatest temperature is 1 degree, and the least is $-4$ degrees. Among the negative readings, $-0.5$ is the greatest because it is nearest zero from the left. If a learner chooses $-4$ as the greatest because 4 has the largest digits, ask them to point to the rightmost plotted value. The number-line definition settles the comparison independently of how many digits appear.

```numberline
{"x":[-5,2],"points":[{"at":[-4,0],"label":"−4"},{"at":[-2.5,0],"label":"−2.5"},{"at":[-0.5,0],"label":"−0.5"},{"at":[1,0],"label":"1"}],"caption":"The readings increase from left to right: negative four, negative two and a half, negative one half, then one."}
```

## Measure distance from zero

The **[[absolute value]]** of a number is its distance from zero on the number line. Vertical bars denote absolute value: $|-8|=8$ and $|3|=3$. Because distance is nonnegative, an absolute value cannot be negative. Zero has absolute value zero. Opposite numbers have equal absolute values, even though they occupy different positions unless both are zero.

A **[[magnitude]]** describes the size of a signed quantity without its direction. In these number-line contexts, absolute value gives that magnitude. A position of $-8$ meters has magnitude 8 meters relative to the reference. A position of 3 meters has magnitude 3 meters. Therefore the first location is farther from the reference, even though its coordinate is the smaller number.

### Example 2: Compare a signed balance and its size

A classroom game records two balances relative to zero points: one player has $-12$ and another has $-5$. The balance $-5$ is greater because it is closer to zero on the negative side. However, the magnitudes are $|-12|=12$ and $|-5|=5$, so the first player's deficit has greater size.

Write both comparisons explicitly: $-12<-5$, while $|-12|>|-5|$. The bars change the quantities being compared from signed balances to distances from zero. If the question asks who has the larger balance, choose the player at $-5$. If it asks whose deficit is larger, compare magnitudes and choose the player at $-12$. The wording determines the mathematical comparison.

## Work with fractions and decimals

To compare $-3/4$ and $-2/3$, use a common denominator: $-3/4=-9/12$ and $-2/3=-8/12$. Negative nine twelfths lies farther left, so $-3/4<-2/3$. Their absolute values reverse that ordering: $3/4>2/3$. You may also use decimal equivalents when they are exact or sufficiently justified, but do not let an early rounding turn unequal values into an apparent tie.

Consider $|-0.25|$ and $|0.2|$. Their values are 0.25 and 0.2, so the first is larger. This does not mean $-0.25>0.2$; every negative number is less than every positive number. Keep the bars visible throughout your work and say “distance from zero” when you need to recover their meaning.

## Explain zero and opposites

The two solutions to “Which numbers are 4 units from zero?” are 4 and $-4$. The statement $|x|=4$ describes both positions. The statement $x=4$ describes only one. For distance zero, there is only the position zero. These observations will help when interpreting graphs and solution sets later, even though this lesson focuses on comparing values rather than solving general absolute-value equations.

## Compare measurements in the same units

Ordering numerical readings assumes compatible units and the same reference. A temperature of negative three degrees on one scale cannot be compared with negative eight on a different scale merely by ordering the written numbers. In this lesson all comparisons use one specified scale. Likewise, distances from zero refer to that scale’s zero. Read the measurement context before using a number-line comparison to make a real-world claim.

## Common mistakes

A larger absolute value does not always mean a greater signed number. Removing a minus sign without explaining distance confuses notation with meaning. Reversing the order of negative decimals because their unsigned parts increase gives incorrect comparisons. Finally, writing $|-3|=-3$ contradicts the definition of distance. Use a reference point and locate the numbers before comparing them.

## Key points

- Greater values lie farther right on a horizontal number line.
- Absolute value measures distance from zero and is nonnegative.
- Compare signed values and magnitudes according to the question's wording.
- Equivalent fraction and decimal forms represent the same point.

lessons.title: Four-quadrant coordinates
lessons.body:
## Use two number lines to locate a point

A number line locates positions along one direction. A map or grid needs two directions. A **[[coordinate plane]]** combines two perpendicular number lines: the horizontal x-axis and the vertical y-axis. They meet at the **[[origin]]**, the point with coordinates $(0,0)$. Each axis has a scale, and its labels tell you how much one interval represents.

The horizontal coordinate tells how far left or right to move from the origin, while the vertical coordinate tells how far up or down to move. Positive x-values point right; negative x-values point left. Positive y-values point up; negative y-values point down. These conventions extend the signed-number ideas from the previous lessons to two dimensions.

## Preserve the order of the coordinates

An **[[ordered pair]]** gives a location as $(x,y)$, with the horizontal coordinate first and vertical coordinate second. To plot $(3,-2)$, begin at the origin, move 3 units right, and then 2 units down. The point is at the intersection of those horizontal and vertical positions. Reversing the coordinates to $(-2,3)$ gives a different point.

You do not have to draw the walking path every time, but the movement description helps interpret the symbols. A coordinate records location, not the total distance traveled to get there. Many routes can reach the same point. Also, the comma separates the two coordinates; it is not a decimal point. Write parentheses so the pair is clearly distinguished from two unrelated numbers.

## Name the four regions

A **[[quadrant]]** is one of the four open regions formed by the axes. Quadrants are numbered counterclockwise starting in the upper right. Quadrant I contains positive x and positive y. Quadrant II contains negative x and positive y. Quadrant III contains negative x and negative y. Quadrant IV contains positive x and negative y.

| Region | Sign of x | Sign of y | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | Positive | Positive | $(2,3)$ |
| II | Negative | Positive | $(-2,3)$ |
| III | Negative | Negative | $(-2,-3)$ |
| IV | Positive | Negative | $(2,-3)$ |

Points on an axis are not in a quadrant. If $x=0$, the point is on the y-axis. If $y=0$, it is on the x-axis. The origin lies on both axes. This distinction matters because a zero coordinate has no positive or negative sign and therefore does not satisfy any quadrant's pair of sign conditions.

### Example 1: Plot and read locations

Plot $A=(3,-2)$ and $B=(-2,3)$. For A, move right 3 and down 2; it lies in Quadrant IV. For B, move left 2 and up 3; it lies in Quadrant II. Both points use the numbers 2 and 3, but their signs and order produce different locations.

```plot
{"x":[-4,4],"y":[-4,4],"equal":true,"points":[{"at":[3,-2],"label":"A (3, −2)"},{"at":[-2,3],"label":"B (−2, 3)"},{"at":[0,-3],"label":"C (0, −3)"}],"xLabel":"x","yLabel":"y","caption":"A lies in Quadrant IV, B in Quadrant II, and C lies on the negative y-axis."}
```

Now read point C at $(0,-3)$. Its x-coordinate is zero, so there is no horizontal displacement from the origin. Its y-coordinate is negative three, so it lies three units down the y-axis. Calling it a Quadrant III point would be incorrect because Quadrant III requires a negative x-coordinate as well as a negative y-coordinate.

### Example 2: Use a scaled map

A park map places the visitor center at the origin. Each grid interval represents 0.5 kilometer. A lookout is four intervals right and three intervals up. The coordinates in kilometers are $(2,1.5)$, because $4\times0.5=2$ and $3\times0.5=1.5$. The lookout lies in Quadrant I.

A campsite is two intervals left and five intervals down. Its coordinates are $(-1,-2.5)$ kilometers, in Quadrant III. Do not report $(-2,-5)$ kilometers unless the axes actually use one kilometer per interval. Counting grid spaces and reading coordinate values are related tasks, but the axis scale connects them.

## Include fractions and decimals

Coordinates need not be integers. The point $(-1.5,2.25)$ lies one and a half units left of the y-axis and two and a quarter units above the x-axis. Subdivide the marked intervals consistently to plot it. A coordinate plane is continuous in this model, so positions exist between drawn grid lines even when the display does not label every fraction.

To check a plotted point, project it horizontally to the y-axis and vertically to the x-axis, then read the corresponding values. Confirm the signs from the quadrant. A point claimed to be $(-1.5,2.25)$ should be in the upper-left region. If your drawing puts it lower right, at least one direction or sign has been reversed.

## Make a map understandable

A coordinate description needs an origin, axis directions, and units. On an abstract mathematical grid, x and y labels may be enough. On a real map, explain what positive directions represent, such as east and north, and how the scale converts grid intervals to distance. Two maps can assign different coordinates to the same physical location if they choose different origins, so coordinates belong to a specified system.

## Common mistakes

Swapping x and y changes most locations. Treating a negative coordinate as a negative distance confuses direction with length. Placing axis points in quadrants ignores the zero coordinate. Finally, assuming one grid interval always represents one unit can multiply every reported location by the wrong factor. Read the axis labels before plotting or interpreting any point.

## Key points

- Ordered pairs list horizontal position first and vertical position second.
- Signs identify directions from the origin and the four quadrants.
- Points with a zero coordinate lie on an axis, outside the quadrants.
- Use the stated scale and units, including fractional positions.

lessons.title: Coordinate distances and contexts
lessons.body:
## Use a shared coordinate to identify direction

Two points with the same y-coordinate lie on one horizontal line. Two points with the same x-coordinate lie on one vertical line. An **[[axis-aligned segment]]** is a segment parallel to one of the coordinate axes. Its length can be found by comparing the one coordinate that changes. You do not need a general diagonal distance formula for these segments.

A **[[horizontal distance]]** compares x-coordinates while y remains fixed. A **[[vertical distance]]** compares y-coordinates while x remains fixed. In either case, distance is nonnegative and carries the coordinate scale's length unit. Coordinates may be negative, but a measured separation cannot be negative. This distinction extends the difference between position and magnitude from the number line.

## Count or compare along one axis

For points $(2,3)$ and $(7,3)$, count from x equals 2 to x equals 7. The length is 5 units. You can calculate $7-2=5$. For points $(-6,3)$ and $(-2,3)$, the length is 4 units because the coordinates are four positions apart. Use a number line if subtraction with negative values feels uncertain; the geometric counting remains valid.

When a segment crosses an axis, add the distances on either side of zero. From $(-4,2)$ to $(3,2)$, travel 4 units from negative four to zero and then 3 more to positive three. The total is 7. This is not the difference between the two absolute values; $4-3=1$ would compare their distances from zero rather than the distance between the points.

### Example 1: Measure a horizontal path

A grid map places a fountain at $(-4,2)$ and a gate at $(3,2)$. Each coordinate unit represents 10 meters. The equal y-coordinates show that the direct path between them is horizontal. Its coordinate length is $4+3=7$ units because it crosses the y-axis. Multiply by the map scale: $7\times10=70$ meters.

```plot
{"x":[-5,4],"y":[-1,4],"equal":true,"points":[{"at":[-4,2],"label":"Fountain"},{"at":[3,2],"label":"Gate"}],"segments":[{"from":[-4,2],"to":[3,2],"label":"7 units"}],"caption":"The horizontal segment from (−4, 2) to (3, 2) has length seven coordinate units."}
```

Check the answer by following the two parts of the route: 40 meters from the fountain to the y-axis, then 30 meters from the axis to the gate. Their total is 70 meters. The y-coordinate 2 locates the path above the x-axis; it does not add another 2 units to this horizontal segment's length.

### Example 2: Measure a vertical path and a route

A lift moves from $(2,-3)$ to $(2,5)$ on a diagram measured in meters. The equal x-coordinates show a vertical segment. It travels 3 meters up to the x-axis and another 5 meters above it, giving 8 meters. The horizontal coordinate stays at 2 throughout the movement and does not contribute to the vertical distance.

Now a walker starts at $(-2,-1)$, goes horizontally to $(3,-1)$, then vertically to $(3,4)$. The first segment is 5 units and the second is 5 units, so this specified route is 10 units long. That is the length of the two-segment route, not a claim about the straight diagonal between the start and finish. Different routes can join the same endpoints with different total lengths.

## Reflect across an axis

A **[[reflection]]** across an axis places a point the same perpendicular distance on the opposite side of that axis. Reflecting $(3,2)$ across the x-axis gives $(3,-2)$: the horizontal location stays 3, while the vertical direction reverses. Reflecting $(3,2)$ across the y-axis gives $(-3,2)$: the vertical location stays 2, while the horizontal direction reverses.

The reflected pair across the x-axis is separated vertically by 4 units, because each point is 2 units from the axis. The reflected pair across the y-axis is separated horizontally by 6 units, because each point is 3 units from that axis. A point already on the reflecting axis stays in place, since its perpendicular distance from that axis is zero.

## Generalize without losing the picture

For an axis-aligned segment, the distance is the absolute value of the difference of the changing coordinates. For x-coordinates $a$ and $b$, write $|b-a|$. This expression produces the same distance if the endpoints are reversed. At this stage, you can still calculate by counting intervals or splitting at zero; the formula summarizes those geometric methods.

Be careful when both coordinates change. The points $(1,1)$ and $(4,5)$ are neither horizontally nor vertically aligned. Adding the horizontal change 3 and vertical change 4 gives a right-angle route length of 7 units, not the direct diagonal length. This lesson makes no claim that every pair of points can be measured by adding coordinate changes. State the route when you use that method.

## Check a contextual model

Map distances require a scale, and a route on a map may not match an available walkway. If a problem specifies an unobstructed horizontal path, the axis-aligned calculation models it directly. If a fence forces a detour, add the lengths of the stated route segments instead. Mathematical coordinates describe a model; the context tells you which segments are meaningful to measure.

## Common mistakes

Subtracting absolute values fails for points on opposite sides of zero. Adding a fixed coordinate to the distance counts a location that never changes. Reporting a negative distance confuses direction with length. Treating a two-segment route as the direct diagonal makes an unsupported claim. Check alignment, scale, and the requested route before calculating.

## Key points

- Equal y-coordinates give horizontal alignment; equal x-coordinates give vertical alignment.
- Measure separation along the changing coordinate and keep distance nonnegative.
- Reflections preserve distance from an axis while reversing the perpendicular coordinate.
- Distinguish a specified route length from the straight distance between endpoints.

lessons.title: Exponents and operation order
lessons.body:
## Record repeated multiplication compactly

An arrangement has four layers, each with four rows of four blocks. Multiplying $4\times4\times4$ counts all the blocks. Exponent notation writes this repeated product as $4^3$. The **[[base]]** is the factor being repeated, and the **[[exponent]]** tells how many times it appears as a factor when the exponent is a positive whole number. In this example, the base is 4 and the exponent is 3.

A **[[power]]** is an expression formed from a base and an exponent, or the value of that expression when the context makes the meaning clear. The power $4^3$ equals 64. It does not equal $4\times3=12$, because the exponent is not another factor in an ordinary two-number multiplication. Expanding the power into repeated factors makes the distinction visible.

## Connect squares and cubes to measurements

A square with side length 5 units has area $5\times5=5^2=25$ square units. A cube with edge length 5 units has volume $5\times5\times5=5^3=125$ cubic units. The words “squared” and “cubed” reflect these geometric relationships. Exponents also describe repeated products without a geometric setting, so $2^4$ is meaningful even when no four-dimensional object is being discussed.

For a positive whole-number exponent of 1, the base appears once: $7^1=7$. For a nonzero base, an exponent of zero gives 1. One way to see this pattern is to divide consecutive powers by the base: $3^3=27$, $3^2=9$, $3^1=3$, and $3^0=1$. Each step divides by 3. This lesson does not assign a value to $0^0$.

## Agree on an operation order

The **[[order of operations]]** is the convention for evaluating expressions consistently. First evaluate grouped expressions, such as parentheses. Then evaluate powers. Next perform multiplication and division from left to right at the same priority. Finally perform addition and subtraction from left to right at the same priority. Grouping symbols can change the order, so read the expression's structure before calculating.

Multiplication does not always happen before division, and addition does not always happen before subtraction. Within either shared-priority pair, work from left to right. Thus $24\div6\times2=4\times2=8$. Multiplying $6\times2$ first would produce $24\div12=2$, which is the value of a differently grouped expression, $24\div(6\times2)$.

### Example 1: Evaluate an expression with a power

Evaluate $3+2^3\times4$. There are no parentheses to handle. First expand or calculate the power: $2^3=2\times2\times2=8$. The expression becomes $3+8\times4$. Next multiply to get $3+32$. Finally add to obtain 35.

Check the structure by reading it as “three more than four copies of eight.” If you add 3 and 2 before handling the power, you change the expression to something else. Recording one operation per line makes the preserved structure visible and helps identify exactly where an error occurs. An equals sign should connect expressions with the same value, so every line in the chain must still equal 35.

### Example 2: Compare grouped and ungrouped expressions

Evaluate $(18-6)\div3+2^2$. The parentheses give 12, and the power gives 4. The expression is now $12\div3+4$. Division gives 4, then addition gives $4+4=8$. Check that the original grouping requires the entire difference 18 minus 6 to be divided by 3.

Now remove those parentheses: $18-6\div3+2^2$. Evaluate the power and division first: $18-2+4$. Addition and subtraction share priority, so move left to right: $16+4=20$. The same numbers and operation symbols produce different answers because the grouping changed. Parentheses communicate a mathematical decision; they are not optional decoration.

## Keep track of a fraction bar

A fraction bar groups its entire numerator and denominator. The expression $(12+6)/3$ means divide the sum 18 by 3, giving 6. In display notation, $\frac{12+6}{3}$ has that same grouping built into the bar. It does not mean $12+(6/3)$, which would equal 14. When entering an expression on a calculator, include parentheses around multi-term numerators and denominators.

Try $30-12+5$. Because addition and subtraction have equal priority, calculate $30-12=18$, then $18+5=23$. Grouping the last two numbers first would instead evaluate $30-(12+5)=13$. You can use a number-line sequence to check the original: begin at 30, move left 12, then right 5. The endpoint is 23.

## Explain an efficient method

Sometimes a property of operations offers an alternative after the expression is understood. To find $5\times(10+2)$, you may calculate the parentheses first and multiply $5\times12=60$. You may also distribute to $50+10=60$. Both methods respect the original grouping because distribution preserves value. The next lessons will formalize those equivalent forms, rather than treating shortcuts as exceptions to the operation convention.

Write a brief explanation with each answer: name the first operation, show the intermediate expression, and check that grouping has been preserved. This is more useful than listing a memorized acronym without indicating which operations share priority. A reader should be able to reproduce your calculation from the lines you show.

## Check a written equality chain

If you evaluate 2 + 3 × 4, do not write 2 + 3 = 5 × 4 = 20. The first equality falsely states that 5 equals 20, and the multiplication should have come first. Write 2 + 3 × 4 = 2 + 12 = 14 instead. Each expression in that chain has one unchanged value. Clear notation supports correct thinking and lets a reviewer locate an error.

## Common mistakes

Multiplying the base by the exponent confuses repeated multiplication with ordinary multiplication. Doing all multiplication before any division misreads equal-priority operations. Adding before subtracting regardless of position makes the same mistake. Dropping parentheses around a fraction's numerator changes its meaning. Expand a power and mark groups before beginning if an expression seems crowded.

## Key points

- Positive whole-number exponents count repeated factors.
- Grouping comes first, followed by powers and then shared-priority operations.
- Work left to right within multiplication/division and addition/subtraction.
- Each equals sign in your working should preserve the expression's value.

lessons.title: Write and evaluate expressions
lessons.body:
## Describe a changing quantity

A notebook costs 3 dollars. One notebook costs 3 dollars, two cost 6 dollars, and five cost 15 dollars. Instead of listing every possible purchase, use a letter to represent the number of notebooks. A **[[variable]]** is a symbol representing a quantity that may be unknown or may take different values. If $n$ is the notebook count, $3n$ represents the cost in dollars.

An **[[algebraic expression]]** combines numbers, variables, and operations without asserting an equality between two sides. The expression $3n+2$ might represent a notebook cost plus a fixed 2-dollar delivery charge. It can be evaluated once a value of $n$ is supplied. An equation, by contrast, states that two expressions are equal; later lessons use equations to find unknown values.

## Name the parts of an expression

A **[[term]]** is a part of an expression separated at the top level by addition or subtraction. In $3n+2$, the terms are $3n$ and 2. The term $3n$ is a product even though its multiplication symbol is omitted. The number 3 is its **[[coefficient]]**, the numerical factor multiplying the variable. The 2 is a fixed number independent of $n$ in this model.

Structure matters when naming parts. In $4(n+2)$, the entire expression is a product of 4 and the grouped sum $n+2$. Inside the parentheses, $n$ and 2 are terms of that sum. Seeing a group as one quantity helps when translating a phrase such as “four times the sum” and when applying distribution in the next lesson.

## Translate words in order

“Five more than a number” becomes $x+5$. “Five less than a number” becomes $x-5$, because the starting quantity is the number and five is removed from it. “Five minus a number” becomes $5-x$. The same words can appear in different relationships, so translation should preserve meaning rather than follow the word order mechanically.

“Three times the sum of a number and two” is $3(x+2)$. “Three times a number, then add two” is $3x+2$. Parentheses distinguish these operations. Test a simple value such as $x=1$: the first expression gives 9 and the second gives 5. Because the results differ, the two phrases cannot be represented by the same expression.

### Example 1: Build and evaluate a cost model

A craft activity charges 4 dollars per kit and a fixed 3-dollar setup charge for the group. Let $k$ be the number of kits purchased. The kits cost $4k$, and adding the fixed charge gives $4k+3$. The fixed charge is added once, not once per kit. This distinction is part of the model, not merely a symbolic choice.

For six kits, substitute 6 for every occurrence of $k$: $4(6)+3=24+3=27$ dollars. Check by a repeated addition interpretation: six kits contribute six copies of 4 dollars, or 24 dollars, plus the one 3-dollar charge. For zero kits, the expression gives 3 dollars, but whether that charge is actually collected with no purchase depends on the stated policy. The model's allowed inputs must fit the situation.

## Substitute carefully

To evaluate an expression, replace each occurrence of the variable with its specified value, preserve grouping, and then use the order of operations. Parentheses around a substituted value make multiplication clear. For $2a^2+1$ at $a=3$, write $2(3)^2+1=2(9)+1=19$. The coefficient 2 is not included in the square unless the expression groups it with the variable.

If an expression uses two variables, substitute both using their separate definitions. In $lw$, the letters may represent a rectangle's length and width. If $l=5.5$ and $w=2$, the area is $5.5\times2=11$ square units. Letters are not automatically abbreviations for objects; they stand for numerical quantities with meanings and units supplied by the problem.

### Example 2: Evaluate a geometric formula

The area of a rectangle is $A=lw$. A drawing has length $l=7.5$ centimeters and width $w=4$ centimeters. Substitute both values: $A=7.5\times4=30$ square centimeters. The product counts how many square-centimeter units cover the rectangle, so the output unit is an area unit.

Its perimeter uses a different expression, $P=2l+2w$. Substitute the same measurements: $P=2(7.5)+2(4)=15+8=23$ centimeters. Using the same inputs does not make the expressions interchangeable. Area measures covering, while perimeter measures boundary length. The output's meaning and unit help determine which expression belongs to the task.

## Make a table of values

For the expression $3n+2$, a small table shows how outputs change with the input. At $n=0$, the output is 2; at $n=1$, it is 5; at $n=2$, it is 8; and at $n=3$, it is 11. Each additional unit of $n$ adds 3 to the output because the coefficient is 3. The fixed 2 contributes to every output but does not change that step size.

Use a table as a check on translation. If a story says there is a one-time charge, the zero-input output often reveals it mathematically. If a story says the total is only a constant price per item, the expression has no extra fixed charge. State restrictions such as whole-number item counts so that a reader knows which substitutions make sense in context.

## Common mistakes

Treating $3n$ as $3+n$ changes multiplication into addition. Reversing “less than” can reverse subtraction. Squaring a coefficient that is outside the power changes the grouping. Substituting for only one occurrence of a variable produces an inconsistent calculation. Finally, using a formula without its units can conceal the difference between area and perimeter.

## Key points

- Define variables with meanings and units before writing an expression.
- Read terms, coefficients, products, and grouped sums as structure.
- Substitute consistently and preserve the order of operations.
- Check the expression against the context and the allowed input values.

lessons.title: Equivalent expressions and distribution
lessons.body:
## Different forms can preserve one value

A row of kits contains 3 pencils and 2 erasers in each kit. For $k$ kits, you can count all five objects per kit using $5k$. You can also count pencils and erasers separately using $3k+2k$. The expressions look different but describe the same total for every permitted kit count. **[[Equivalent expressions]]** have the same value for every value of their variables in the domain being considered.

Agreement at one input is not enough to prove equivalence. The expressions $x+2$ and $2x$ both equal 4 when $x=2$, but at $x=3$ they give 5 and 6. A counterexample shows they are not equivalent. Properties of operations explain why an equivalence holds across all permitted inputs instead of merely checking a few selected cases.

## Rearrange and regroup with care

The **[[commutative property]]** of addition or multiplication allows the order of operands to change: $a+b=b+a$ and $ab=ba$. The **[[associative property]]** allows grouping to change within addition or multiplication: $(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)$ and $(ab)c=a(bc)$. These properties do not generally apply to subtraction or division. For example, $8-3$ and $3-8$ do not have equal values.

Use these properties to make a calculation clearer without changing its operations. The sum $17+8+3$ can be regrouped as $(17+3)+8=28$. The product $4\times7\times25$ can be rearranged as $(4\times25)\times7=700$. Explain which operation allows the change, rather than assuming every reordering is permitted.

## Distribute multiplication across a sum

The **[[distributive property]]** connects multiplication with addition: $a(b+c)=ab+ac$. A rectangle with height $a$ and widths $b$ and $c$ can be viewed as one large rectangle or two smaller rectangles. The total area is unchanged, which gives a visual reason that both terms inside the parentheses must be multiplied by $a$.

```shape
{"polygons":[{"points":[[0,0],[5,0],[5,3],[0,3]]}],"segments":[{"from":[2,0],"to":[2,3]},{"from":[0,0],"to":[2,0],"label":"b"},{"from":[2,0],"to":[5,0],"label":"c"},{"from":[0,0],"to":[0,3],"label":"a"}],"caption":"A rectangle of height a is split into widths b and c. Its area can be written a(b + c) or ab + ac."}
```

Distribution also works over subtraction: $a(b-c)=ab-ac$. Think of removing a rectangular piece from a larger rectangle when the lengths make that picture possible. The algebraic property describes equivalent expressions even when a particular area drawing is not the most useful model. At this level, use nonnegative lengths for literal geometric examples.

### Example 1: Expand a grouped expression

Rewrite $4(x+3)$ without parentheses. The 4 multiplies both terms in the sum: $4x+4\times3=4x+12$. A common incorrect result is $4x+3$, which multiplies only the first term. Test $x=2$ to see the error: the original gives $4(5)=20$, while $4(2)+3=11$.

The correct expanded expression gives $4(2)+12=20$. This substitution checks the example, but the distributive property supplies the general reason for equivalence. You can also imagine four groups, each containing $x$ objects and 3 more objects. Across the four groups there are four copies of $x$ and twelve additional objects.

### Example 2: Combine matching variable parts

Simplify $3x+2x+7$. The first two terms both count copies of the same quantity $x$. Use distribution backward: $3x+2x=(3+2)x=5x$. The expression becomes $5x+7$. The constant 7 cannot be added to the coefficient 5 to give $12x$, because it does not represent seven copies of $x$.

At $x=4$, the original expression gives $12+8+7=27$, and the simplified expression gives $20+7=27$. The incorrect $12x$ would give 48. A unit interpretation helps: three bundles of $x$ objects plus two bundles of $x$ objects make five bundles, while seven loose objects remain separate. Combining terms requires matching variable structure, not merely nearby numbers.

## Explain non-equivalence

Compare $2(x+5)$ with $2x+5$. Expand the first to $2x+10$. The constant parts differ by 5 for every value of $x$, so the expressions are not equivalent. A single test value, such as zero, is enough to disprove a claimed equivalence: the first gives 10 and the second gives 5. It takes a general property or argument to establish equivalence for all values.

Now compare $6x+9$ with $3(2x+3)$. Distribution gives $3(2x)+3(3)=6x+9$, so the expressions are equivalent. The grouped form may reveal three equal groups, while the expanded form may make substitution easier. “Simpler” depends partly on the task; the central requirement is preserving value.

## Apply properties to mental arithmetic

To calculate $7\times19$, write $19=20-1$ and distribute: $7(20-1)=140-7=133$. To calculate $25\times12$, use $25(8+4)=200+100=300$, or regroup $25\times(3\times4)=(25\times4)\times3=300$. These methods use different properties but reach the same value. State enough steps that another learner can see why the transformation is valid.

When a variable stands for a measured quantity, keep its meaning consistent across the expression. Combining $3x+2y$ as $5x$ would silently assume that $x$ and $y$ represent the same value. Without that information, the expressions need not agree. Matching letters and powers matter because they identify what is being counted or scaled.

## Use a counterexample deliberately

A good test value is easy to calculate and distinguishes the proposed forms. To examine 2x + 3 versus 5x, avoid choosing x = 1 because both happen to equal 5 there. Choose x = 0: the first gives 3 and the second gives 0. This disproves equivalence immediately. Testing zero is especially useful when a mistaken rewrite merges a constant into a variable coefficient. Testing another value can then help explain the pattern, but the single differing result already settles the false universal claim.

## Common mistakes

Distributing to only one term changes the expression. Combining constants with variable coefficients confuses unlike quantities. Applying commutativity to subtraction or division reverses an operation that depends on order. Finally, declaring equivalence after one matching substitution overlooks other inputs. Use properties to justify transformations and counterexamples to reject false ones.

## Key points

- Equivalent expressions agree for every permitted variable value.
- Addition and multiplication allow specific rearrangements and regroupings.
- Distribution multiplies every term inside a group.
- Combine matching variable parts and keep unlike parts distinct.

lessons.title: Common factors in expressions
lessons.body:
## Read distribution in reverse

The expression $12x+18$ can describe twelve copies of a quantity plus eighteen additional units. It can also describe six equal groups, each containing $2x+3$. Writing $12x+18=6(2x+3)$ is an example of **[[factoring]]**, rewriting an expression as a product of factors. Factoring does not change the expression's value; it reveals a multiplication structure that may be less visible in the original sum.

This connects to the greatest-common-factor work with whole numbers. Since 6 divides both 12 and 18, it can be taken as a shared multiplier. The remaining terms come from division: $12x/6=2x$ and $18/6=3$. If the outside factor multiplies the parentheses back to the original expression, the rewrite is correct.

## Compare expanded and factored forms

An **[[expanded form]]** displays the separate terms obtained after multiplication is distributed. A **[[factored form]]** displays an expression as a product. For example, $5x+20$ is expanded and $5(x+4)$ is factored. Neither is automatically better in every situation. The expanded form may make addition of matching terms convenient; the factored form may show equal groups or simplify a mental calculation.

A **[[common factor of terms]]** divides every term in an expression. In $12x+18$, the whole-number common factors include 1, 2, 3, and 6. Factoring out 2 gives $2(6x+9)$, which is correct. Factoring out 6 gives $6(2x+3)$, where the remaining numerical coefficients share no factor greater than one. At this stage, we focus on extracting positive whole-number factors.

### Example 1: Factor a two-term expression

Factor $12x+18$ using the greatest common factor of its numerical coefficients. The greatest common factor of 12 and 18 is 6. Divide each term by 6: $12x/6=2x$ and $18/6=3$. Place those results inside parentheses and put 6 outside, giving $6(2x+3)$.

Check by distributing: $6(2x+3)=6(2x)+6(3)=12x+18$. For a numerical check at $x=2$, the original gives $24+18=42$ and the factored expression gives $6(4+3)=42$. The distribution check proves the equivalence generally; the substitution check helps catch an arithmetic mistake in this particular expression.

An incorrect rewrite is $6(2x+18)$. Its expansion is $12x+108$, not the original expression. That error comes from dividing only the variable term while leaving the constant unchanged. Every term inside the parentheses must be the corresponding original term divided by the outside factor.

## Use grouping meaningfully

Suppose a class prepares six identical stations. Each station needs $2x$ small pieces and 3 large pieces. The total number of pieces is $6(2x+3)$. Expanding gives $12x+18$, which separates all the small pieces from all the large pieces. Both forms describe the same collection, but the grouped form directly shows what belongs at each station.

If $x$ counts a whole number of sets, the context restricts it to nonnegative whole numbers. Algebraic equivalence itself is broader than that particular interpretation. You can evaluate both forms at other numerical inputs to study the relationship, but you should not claim that a fractional station supply count is physically possible unless the items or units can be divided.

### Example 2: Factor and calculate efficiently

Find the value of $18\times7+18\times3$. The two products share a factor of 18. Factor it out: $18(7+3)$. The sum inside is 10, so the value is $18\times10=180$. This avoids separately computing 126 and 54, although adding those products also gives 180.

Now consider the expression $8y+12$. The greatest common factor of 8 and 12 is 4, so write $4(2y+3)$. If $y=5$, the value is $4(10+3)=52$. The original gives $8(5)+12=40+12=52$. A common factor helps both expose structure and organize evaluation; it is not a new arithmetic operation with unrelated rules.

## Work with more than two terms

For $6a+9b+12$, the greatest common numerical factor is 3. Divide every term by 3 to obtain $3(2a+3b+4)$. The letters a and b need not represent the same quantity, so the terms cannot simply be combined into one variable term. Factoring a shared number does not require all terms to have the same variable structure.

A subtraction example works similarly: $15z-10=5(3z-2)$. Keep the subtraction sign between the resulting terms. Distributing back gives $15z-10$. At $z=2$, both forms give 20. If the expression is used to count objects in a context, choose permitted values that keep its interpretation sensible, while preserving the algebraic sign accurately in the rewrite.

## Decide whether a larger factor remains

The form $2(6x+9)$ correctly factors $12x+18$, but the inside coefficients 6 and 9 still share 3. Factoring that shared 3 yields $2\times3(2x+3)=6(2x+3)$. If a question explicitly requests the greatest common factor, stop only after extracting that greatest shared numerical factor. If it asks for any equivalent product, the earlier correct form may already answer it.

Use size checks on the coefficients. Dividing a positive coefficient by a factor greater than one should make it smaller. If extracting 4 from $8y+12$ leaves 32y inside, the operation has been reversed. Multiplying the proposed factors back is the most direct way to verify and explain a correction.

## Common mistakes

Removing a factor from just one term changes the value. Leaving out parentheses can make the outside factor apply to only the first term. Confusing a common factor with a common multiple produces unsuitable outside numbers for whole-number factoring. Finally, declaring a correct but non-greatest factorization wrong overlooks the question's wording; distinguish “equivalent” from “using the greatest common factor.”

## Key points

- Factoring reverses distribution and rewrites a sum as a product.
- Divide every term by the extracted common factor.
- The greatest common numerical factor gives coefficients with no larger shared whole-number factor.
- Expand the result to verify equivalence and explain what the groups represent.

lessons.title: Equality and solutions
lessons.body:
## Equality compares two values

The statement $8+4=12$ says that the expression on the left and the expression on the right have the same value. The **[[equals sign]]** expresses that relationship; it does not merely announce that an answer is coming next. Because equality works in both directions, $12=8+4$ is equally valid. So is $8+4=7+5$, since both sides evaluate to 12.

An **[[equation]]** is a statement asserting that two expressions are equal. Some equations are true, some are false, and equations with variables may be true for certain inputs but false for others. The equation $x+4=12$ asks us to consider which value of $x$ makes the equality true. It is different from the expression $x+4$, which alone makes no assertion.

## Test a proposed value

A **[[solution]]** of an equation is a value that makes it true when substituted for the variable. For $x+4=12$, the value 8 is a solution because $8+4=12$. The value 7 is not a solution because $7+4=11$, and 11 is not equal to 12. The test compares both evaluated sides; it does not depend on whether a value merely looks reasonable.

**[[Substitution]]** replaces a variable with a specified value while preserving every operation and grouping symbol. If the variable appears more than once, replace it consistently everywhere. For $2x+1=x+5$, testing $x=4$ gives $2(4)+1=4+5$, or $9=9$. That confirms 4 is a solution without requiring a general method for solving every equation of that form.

## Read a missing-number statement

The equation $9+\square=15$ and the equation $9+x=15$ ask the same missing-number question. The variable provides a flexible symbol that can appear in several connected statements. Think about what the equation says before choosing an operation. “Nine plus what amount equals fifteen?” suggests that the missing amount is the difference between 15 and 9.

A balance picture can help. Imagine that each side represents the total weight on one side of a balanced scale. If the totals are equal, the scale is level. A proposed variable value replaces an unknown weight. If the replacement makes one side heavier, it is not a solution. The picture communicates equality even when no physical scale is present.

### Example 1: Test a set of candidates

Determine which of 4, 5, and 6 solves $3n=15$. For $n=4$, the left side is $3\times4=12$, while the right side remains 15. Since 12 and 15 differ, 4 is not a solution. For $n=5$, the left side is $3\times5=15$, so both sides agree. For $n=6$, the left side is 18, which does not equal 15.

Therefore 5 is the solution among the listed candidates. The variable represents the number in each of three equal groups if 15 is their total. You can also reason backward from multiplication: $15\div3=5$. Testing all candidates provides evidence for the selection, while the grouping interpretation explains why division is a useful solving operation.

| Candidate n | Left side 3n | Right side | Equal? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 12 | 15 | No |
| 5 | 15 | 15 | Yes |
| 6 | 18 | 15 | No |

### Example 2: Interpret an equation in context

A student has read 18 pages and has $r$ pages remaining in a 50-page section. The equation is $18+r=50$. The variable measures remaining pages, so an allowed value is a nonnegative whole number. Test $r=32$: $18+32=50$, so it satisfies the equation and the context.

Test $r=50$: $18+50=68$, which is not the section total. This error treats the whole as though it were the remaining part. The solution 32 pages answers the original question, while the equation records how completed and remaining pages combine. Reading the variable definition after solving is a useful way to write a meaningful final sentence.

## An equation may have different solution behavior

The equation $x+0=x$ is true for every value for which the arithmetic is defined, because adding zero changes nothing. By contrast, $x+1=x$ is not true for any ordinary rational value of $x$. An equation such as $x+4=12$ has exactly one rational solution. These observations remind you that the presence of an equals sign does not guarantee one particular answer pattern.

You do not need a new general solving procedure to verify these simple cases. Use meanings: adding zero leaves a quantity unchanged, while adding one increases it. For candidate-based questions, test each listed value and report those that make the statement true. Later algebra will develop systematic methods for classifying more complicated equations.

## Keep written steps truthful

Suppose you calculate the total $6+4+3$. A correct chain is $6+4+3=10+3=13$. The chain $6+4=10+3=13$ is incorrect because it asserts that 10 equals 13 at its first link. Use separate lines if a running calculation would otherwise misuse the equals sign. Every equality should compare complete expressions with the same value.

When checking a solution with decimals or fractions, preserve exact values when possible. For $x+0.25=1$, testing $x=0.75$ gives exactly 1. For $2x=1$, testing $x=1/2$ gives exactly 1. Solutions are not restricted to whole numbers unless the context says the variable counts indivisible objects.

## Common mistakes

Treating the equals sign as “calculate next” permits false chains. Testing a value in only one occurrence of a variable produces a different equation. Confusing the whole with a missing part gives an answer that fails substitution. Finally, rejecting a fraction just because it is not an integer ignores equations about measurable quantities. Check both the equality and the variable's meaning.

## Key points

- Equality means that two complete expressions have the same value.
- A solution makes an equation true under consistent substitution.
- Test both sides and respect any contextual restrictions on inputs.
- Use equations to represent relationships before solving for an unknown.

lessons.title: One-step equations
lessons.body:
## Undo an operation while preserving equality

Testing candidates is useful, but a solving method can find an unknown directly. An **[[inverse operation]]** reverses another operation: subtraction reverses addition, and division by a nonzero number reverses multiplication by that number. To solve $x+7=19$, undo the added 7. The result is $x=12$, and substitution checks that $12+7=19$.

The **[[balance property of equality]]** says that applying the same valid operation to both sides preserves equality. If two amounts are equal, removing 7 from each leaves equal amounts. Dividing both equal amounts into the same positive number of equal groups also preserves equality. This reasoning explains why an equation's operation must be applied to both sides, rather than only to the side containing the variable.

## Solve an addition relationship

An **[[addition equation]]** in this lesson has the form $x+p=q$, with nonnegative rational values in the situation. Subtract $p$ from both sides to isolate $x$: $x=q-p$. The result must fit any context restrictions. If the task models a remaining count, it should not produce a negative number of objects. A negative result may signal inconsistent given information or a model outside the current context.

Write both sides at every step. From $x+7=19$, write $x+7-7=19-7$, then simplify to $x=12$. Once the reasoning is familiar, you may shorten the written step to $x=19-7=12$, but the balanced operation still justifies it. Moving a number across an equals sign is a shorthand description, not a separate magical rule.

### Example 1: Find a remaining length

A ribbon is 8.5 meters long. A used section measures 3.75 meters, and $r$ meters remain. The equation is $r+3.75=8.5$. Subtract 3.75 from both sides: $r=8.50-3.75=4.75$. The answer is 4.75 meters remaining.

Check by adding the used and remaining amounts: $3.75+4.75=8.50$ meters. Estimate as well: about 4 meters used from about 8.5 leaves about 4.5, so 4.75 is plausible. Adding 3.75 to 8.5 would give 12.25, larger than the original ribbon, which would not make sense for an unaltered remaining section.

The decimal computation is ordinary place-value subtraction. Equation solving does not replace those arithmetic skills; it determines which calculation is needed and why. Keep the variable's unit in the final sentence even when intermediate algebra uses only numbers.

## Solve a multiplication relationship

A **[[multiplication equation]]** in this lesson has the form $px=q$, where $p$ is nonzero. Divide both sides by $p$ to get $x=q/p$. For $6x=42$, division by 6 gives $x=7$. Think of 42 objects split among six equal groups: each group contains seven. Multiplication back verifies $6\times7=42$.

The coefficient can be a positive fraction or decimal. For $0.4x=6$, divide 6 by 0.4 to obtain 15. Because 0.4 is less than one, the whole $x$ is larger than the known part 6. This matches the percent lesson's inverse calculation: 40 percent of a whole is 6, so the whole is 15.

### Example 2: Solve with a fractional coefficient

Three quarters of a container's capacity is 9 liters. Let $c$ be the full capacity in liters. The equation is $(3/4)c=9$. Divide both sides by $3/4$: $c=9\div(3/4)=9\times(4/3)=12$. The full capacity is 12 liters.

Check by finding three quarters of 12: $(3/4)\times12=9$. A unit-fraction approach gives the same reasoning: if three quarter-parts contain 9 liters, one quarter-part contains 3 liters, so all four parts contain 12 liters. This links the formal equation method to a concrete equal-group model and explains why multiplication by the reciprocal works.

## Interpret division equations too

An equation such as $x/5=3.2$ says that one fifth of the unknown is 3.2. Multiply both sides by 5 to recover the whole: $x=16$. Check $16/5=3.2$. Similarly, $x-4=9$ can be solved by adding 4 to both sides, giving 13. These are the same inverse-operation ideas applied to the other direction of the relationship.

Do not divide by zero. The equation $0x=7$ cannot have a solution because zero times any rational number is zero. The equation $0x=0$ is true for every rational value, so it does not determine one unknown. Our ordinary one-step multiplication method assumes a nonzero coefficient precisely to avoid these cases.

## Check method, value, and context

After solving, perform three checks. First, confirm that the same operation was applied to both sides. Second, substitute the result into the original equation, not merely a rewritten version that might already contain an error. Third, read the variable definition to make sure the value is permitted. A fractional length is reasonable, while a fractional count of indivisible tickets may not be.

For example, $4n=18$ gives $n=4.5$. As pure arithmetic, that is correct. If $n$ is liters in each of four equal containers, it is reasonable. If $n$ is the number of whole students in each of four equal groups, the original task cannot be satisfied exactly. Solving reveals this limitation rather than authorizing silent rounding.

## Compare a solution with an estimate

For 0.5x = 11, half of the unknown equals 11, so the full unknown should be about twice 11. Division gives x = 22, agreeing with that estimate. A result of 5.5 would instead be half of 11 and would fail the original equation. This simple meaning check is especially useful when a fractional coefficient makes the operation direction feel unfamiliar.

## Common mistakes

Using the same operation instead of its inverse can increase the unwanted term. Changing only one side breaks equality. Dividing by a fraction without using its reciprocal gives the wrong whole. Rounding a contextually impossible count conceals a model problem. Always return to the original relationship to check both numerical accuracy and meaning.

## Key points

- Inverse operations isolate an unknown by reversing its relationship.
- Apply the same valid operation to both sides of an equation.
- Nonnegative fractions and decimals can be valid solutions.
- Substitute into the original equation and interpret the result in context.

lessons.title: Inequalities and solution sets
lessons.body:
## Describe more than one possible value

A room can hold at most 30 people. Many counts satisfy that rule: 0, 1, 2, and so on through 30. An equation such as $n=30$ would describe only a full room, not every allowed count. An **[[inequality]]** compares quantities using a relation such as less than, greater than, less than or equal to, or greater than or equal to.

The symbols $<$ and $>$ exclude equality. The symbols $\leq$ and $\geq$ include equality. “At most 30” means $n\leq30$, while “more than 30” means $n>30$. The difference at the boundary is essential: exactly 30 people satisfies the first statement but not the second. Translate the wording before selecting a symbol.

## Identify a solution set

A **[[solution set]]** is the collection of all values that make a condition true. For $x>4$ over rational numbers, 5, 4.5, and 100 are solutions, but 4 and 3.9 are not. There are infinitely many rational solutions because between 4 and 5 alone there are endlessly many fractions greater than 4. A number-line ray represents this continuing set without listing each member.

Context may restrict the permitted values. If $n$ counts people, use nonnegative integers. If $t$ measures elapsed time, nonnegative fractions and decimals may make sense. The inequality supplies one condition; the variable's definition supplies others. A graph of all rational values satisfying a comparison is different from a display of only allowed whole-number counts.

## Show whether the endpoint is included

An **[[open endpoint]]** on a number line excludes the boundary value. Draw an open circle at 4 for $x>4$, then extend the ray right to show values greater than 4. A **[[closed endpoint]]** includes the boundary value. Draw a filled point at 4 for $x\geq4$, with the ray again extending right.

For $x<4$ or $x\leq4$, the ray extends left because smaller values lie to the left. The circle's fill communicates inclusion, while the ray's direction communicates order. These are separate decisions. First decide whether equality is allowed; then decide which side contains valid test values.

```numberline
{"x":[0,8],"points":[{"at":[4,0],"open":true,"label":"4"}],"segments":[{"from":[4,0],"to":[8,0],"arrow":true}],"caption":"x is greater than 4: an open endpoint excludes 4, and a rightward ray represents larger values."}
```

### Example 1: Translate and test a capacity rule

A small workshop allows at most 12 participants. Let $n$ be the participant count. “At most” includes 12 and any smaller allowed count, so write $n\leq12$. Because participants are whole people, the contextual solution set is the integers from 0 through 12. A negative count or a count of 3.5 is not permitted even though it is numerically less than 12.

Test the boundary: $12\leq12$ is true. Test one value beyond it: $13\leq12$ is false. Test an interior allowed value: $8\leq12$ is true. These checks confirm the symbol choice. A continuous leftward ray would represent the pure numerical inequality, but for the actual workshop count you would mark only the thirteen permitted integer points.

### Example 2: Model a minimum measurement

A project requires a ribbon at least 2.5 meters long. Let $r$ be the ribbon length in meters. “At least” includes the minimum itself, so write $r\geq2.5$. A 2.5-meter ribbon qualifies, a 2.6-meter ribbon qualifies, and a 2.4-meter ribbon does not. Fractions of a meter are meaningful because length is a continuous measurement in this model.

On a number line, put a closed point at 2.5 and extend right. There is no single largest solution unless another condition gives a maximum. The inequality describes a whole range of acceptable lengths. If the wording were “longer than 2.5 meters,” the endpoint would instead be open, and an exactly 2.5-meter ribbon would fail the condition.

## Use the graph to read a rule

Suppose a number line has an open endpoint at $-2$ and a ray extending left. The graph represents $x<-2$. A test value such as $-3$ confirms the direction because $-3$ is less than $-2$. Zero lies to the right and does not qualify. Negative thresholds still follow the ordinary number-line order; a larger absolute value does not necessarily mean a greater signed number.

Now consider a closed endpoint at 7 with a rightward ray. The rule is $x\geq7$. The endpoint tells you to include equality, and the direction tells you to include larger numbers. Describe both features in words if writing the symbol is difficult. That explanation is enough to reconstruct the graph accurately.

## Distinguish a few examples from all solutions

Listing 5, 6, and 7 as solutions to $x>4$ gives examples but not the full solution set. It omits fractions such as 4.1 and larger numbers such as 1000. A ray or an inequality communicates the unlimited extent. Conversely, a finite contextual set, such as allowed participant counts up to 12, can be listed completely.

When explaining why a value is excluded, identify the violated condition. A value of 13 exceeds the workshop capacity. A value of 3.5 is within the numerical capacity but violates the whole-person requirement. These are different reasons, and naming them helps clarify how mathematical conditions combine with real-world meanings.

## Common mistakes

Using an equation for a range leaves out valid values. Mixing up “at least” and “at most” reverses the ray. Filling an endpoint for a strict inequality wrongly includes the boundary. Finally, assuming every numerical solution is contextually allowed can produce negative counts or fractional people. Test the boundary and one value on each side, then apply the variable's restrictions.

## Key points

- Inequalities describe comparisons and often many possible values.
- Open endpoints exclude equality; closed endpoints include it.
- Ray direction follows number-line order, including negative thresholds.
- A contextual solution set must satisfy both the inequality and the variable's meaning.

lessons.title: Dependent and independent quantities
lessons.body:
## Describe how one quantity changes with another

A machine fills bottles at a constant rate of 3 bottles per minute. After one minute it has filled 3 bottles; after two minutes, 6; after five minutes, 15. The elapsed time is an **[[independent quantity]]**, the input chosen or observed to determine another quantity in the model. The bottle count is the **[[dependent quantity]]**, the output determined from that input.

These names describe roles in a particular relationship. They do not mean that one quantity is unimportant or that a real-world cause has been scientifically proved. A model may use time to calculate distance, or it may rearrange the same relationship to calculate time from distance. Always define which quantity is being treated as input for the current question.

## Write an equation connecting the quantities

An **[[equation model]]** uses an equality to express a relationship between quantities. If $t$ is time in minutes and $b$ is the number of bottles filled in the ideal constant-rate model, write $b=3t$. The coefficient 3 has units of bottles per minute. Multiplying by minutes gives bottles, so the units agree with the output definition.

An **[[allowed input]]** is a value permitted by the model and its context. For elapsed time, negative values are not allowed. If the machine is observed only at whole-minute checkpoints, the displayed inputs might be 0, 1, 2, and so on. A continuous-rate model can describe intermediate times, but actual completed bottle counts require care because bottles are indivisible. State the intended interpretation.

## Make a table and a graph

A table pairs each input with its corresponding output. For $b=3t$, substitute each chosen value of $t$. Include zero when it makes sense: at time zero, before filling begins, the model gives zero bottles. This starting point distinguishes a pure rate model from a situation with an initial amount already present.

| Time t in minutes | Bottle count b |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 3 |
| 2 | 6 |
| 3 | 9 |
| 4 | 12 |

Plot each row as an ordered pair $(t,b)$, placing the input on the horizontal axis and the output on the vertical axis. Label both axes with quantities and units. The point $(2,6)$ means that after two minutes, the modeled count is six bottles. It does not mean six minutes produces two bottles.

### Example 1: Connect all three representations

A cart moves at a constant speed of 3 meters per second from a starting position labeled zero. Let $t$ be elapsed seconds and $d$ be distance traveled in meters. The equation is $d=3t$. At $t=0,1,2,3,4$, the distances are $0,3,6,9,12$. These values form a table and the plotted points $(0,0)$, $(1,3)$, $(2,6)$, $(3,9)$, and $(4,12)$.

```plot
{"x":[0,5],"y":[0,15],"functions":[{"f":"3*x","label":"d = 3t"}],"points":[{"at":[2,6],"label":"2 s, 6 m"}],"xLabel":"Time (seconds)","yLabel":"Distance (meters)","caption":"At constant speed three meters per second, distance equals three times elapsed time and the graph begins at the origin."}
```

The graph is continuous over the modeled time interval because the cart can be observed between whole seconds. At 2.5 seconds, the model gives $3\times2.5=7.5$ meters. A table may list only a few points while the equation describes all allowed times. Extending the line beyond the interval assumes that the same speed continues; the graph alone does not guarantee that real motion will do so.

## Recognize an initial amount

Not every relationship starts at zero. A container already holds 5 liters before water is added at 2 liters per minute. If $t$ is elapsed time and $v$ is volume, the model is $v=2t+5$. The output at zero is 5, and every additional minute adds 2. The constant term represents the initial amount; the coefficient represents the rate of change in this context.

### Example 2: Read a table with a starting value

A table lists times 0, 1, 2, and 3 minutes with volumes 5, 7, 9, and 11 liters. The output increases by 2 for every increase of 1 in the input. The initial output is 5. These observations support $v=2t+5$ over the stated constant-filling period. At four minutes, the predicted volume is $2(4)+5=13$ liters.

Check each row: at zero, the equation gives 5; at one, it gives 7; at two, it gives 9; at three, it gives 11. The rule $v=2t$ has the right step size but misses every row by 5 liters because it omits the initial amount. The ratio $v/t$ is not constant here, so this is not the same pure proportional pattern as $d=3t$.

## Read a graph as a relationship

To find an output from a graph, locate the input on the horizontal axis, move to the plotted relationship, and read the vertical value. To find an input corresponding to a known output, reverse that reading process. In the cart model, a distance of 12 meters corresponds to four seconds because $12=3(4)$. This is also a one-step equation calculation.

A graph must state its scale. Equal visual spacing may represent one second horizontally and three meters vertically. Compare labeled values rather than assuming equal units on both axes. Also distinguish data points from a claimed rule: a few observed pairs may suggest a pattern, but extending it requires an assumption that the relationship continues.

## Common mistakes

Swapping coordinates reverses input and output. Dropping an initial amount gives a rule with the correct change but wrong values. Assuming every table is proportional overlooks nonzero starting outputs. Connecting discrete object counts without explanation can imply impossible fractional objects. State the quantities, units, input restrictions, and constant-rate assumption before using a table or graph to predict.

## Key points

- Define the input and output roles for the relationship.
- Tables, equations, and graphs can represent the same paired values.
- A coefficient may describe a rate, while a constant may describe an initial amount.
- Predictions depend on allowed inputs and the model's stated assumptions.

lessons.title: Area of triangles and quadrilaterals
lessons.body:
## Measure covering with equal squares

**[[Area]]** measures how much two-dimensional space a region covers. A **[[square unit]]** is the area of a square whose sides are one chosen length unit. A rectangle 6 centimeters long and 4 centimeters wide contains six columns of four square centimeters, so its area is $6\times4=24$ square centimeters. The units are squared because two perpendicular lengths are multiplied.

Area differs from boundary length. A narrow rectangle and a compact rectangle can have equal areas but different perimeters. Before selecting a formula, decide whether the task asks for covering, edging, or some other measurement. A material used to cover a floor is modeled by area; a strip around its boundary is modeled by perimeter.

## Use a base and perpendicular height

For a chosen base side, the **[[perpendicular height]]** is the distance to the opposite parallel side or vertex measured at a right angle to the base line. It need not be the length of a slanted edge. A **[[parallelogram]]** is a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. Its area equals base times perpendicular height, just as a rectangle's does.

Why does that formula work? Cut a triangular piece from one side of a parallelogram and slide it to the other side. The pieces form a rectangle with the same base and height, without gaps or overlaps. Rearranging preserves area. The slanted side helps define the shape but does not count how many perpendicular rows of unit squares fit between the parallel bases.

## Derive the triangle formula

Two congruent copies of a triangle can form a parallelogram with the same base and height as the triangle. The parallelogram's area is $bh$, so one triangle has area $A=bh/2$. The factor one half is necessary because the triangle occupies one of the two equal pieces. The argument works for right, acute, and obtuse triangles when the corresponding perpendicular height is used.

A triangle's height can fall outside the drawn triangle for some choices of base. Extend the base line if needed to locate the perpendicular. Do not replace the height with a nearby slanted side just because that side is easier to see. A diagram should label which segment meets the base at a right angle.

### Example 1: Compare a triangle and a parallelogram

A triangle has base 8 centimeters and perpendicular height 5 centimeters. Multiply to get $8\times5=40$ square centimeters, then divide by 2: $A=20$ square centimeters. A parallelogram with the same base and height has area 40 square centimeters. The triangle's area is half as large, consistent with the two-copy argument.

```shape
{"polygons":[{"points":[[0,0],[8,0],[3,5]]}],"segments":[{"from":[0,0],"to":[8,0],"label":"8 cm"},{"from":[3,0],"to":[3,5],"label":"5 cm"}],"rightAngles":[[[3,0],[8,0],[3,5]]],"caption":"A triangle has base eight centimeters and a perpendicular height of five centimeters drawn from its top vertex to the base."}
```

Check the scale of the answer: a surrounding 8-by-5 rectangle has area 40, so the triangle should cover less than that. If you obtained 40 for the triangle, you likely omitted the one-half factor. If you obtained 13, you probably added the dimensions, producing a length-like number rather than a covering measure.

## Decompose quadrilaterals

A quadrilateral can often be split into triangles or rectangles with known dimensions. Add the areas of pieces that cover the region without overlap. If you begin with a larger enclosing rectangle, subtract the unwanted pieces instead. State exactly which pieces are included so that no area is counted twice or omitted.

A trapezoid with parallel base lengths $b_1$ and $b_2$ and perpendicular height $h$ has area $(b_1+b_2)h/2$. One explanation uses two congruent trapezoids to form a parallelogram with base $b_1+b_2$ and height $h$. Divide its area by two to obtain the original trapezoid. Only the parallel sides are the two bases in this formula.

### Example 2: Find a trapezoid's area

A trapezoid has parallel sides of 6 meters and 10 meters, separated by a perpendicular distance of 4 meters. Add the bases: $6+10=16$ meters. Multiply by the height to get $16\times4=64$ square meters, then divide by two. The area is 32 square meters.

Check with a decomposition when the shorter base is centered above the longer one. The middle rectangle has area $6\times4=24$. The two side triangles together have total base length $10-6=4$ and height 4, so together their area is $(4\times4)/2=8$. Add $24+8=32$. The second method explains the same result by visible pieces.

## Work with fractional measurements

The formulas do not require whole-number lengths. A triangle with base 3.5 centimeters and height 2 centimeters has area $(3.5\times2)/2=3.5$ square centimeters. A parallelogram with base $5/2$ meters and height $3/2$ meters has area $15/4$ square meters. Fraction multiplication describes partial unit squares just as whole-number multiplication describes complete rows.

Keep units consistent before multiplying. A base in centimeters and height in meters cannot be multiplied as raw numbers and then labeled square centimeters. Convert one measurement so both lengths use the same unit. For instance, 0.5 meter is 50 centimeters, so a 20-centimeter base and 0.5-meter height give a triangle area of $20\times50/2=500$ square centimeters.

## Common mistakes

Using a slanted edge as height ignores perpendicular separation. Forgetting the one-half factor doubles a triangle's area. Adding all four sides measures perimeter, not area. Applying the trapezoid formula to nonparallel sides uses the wrong bases. Finally, labeling area in ordinary centimeters omits the fact that the measurement counts square units.

## Key points

- Area counts covering in square units and is different from boundary length.
- Rectangle and parallelogram area is base times perpendicular height.
- A triangle has half the area of a corresponding parallelogram.
- Decompose shapes without overlap, and use consistent length units before calculating.

lessons.title: Polygons on coordinates
lessons.body:
## Turn locations into a shape

A **[[polygon]]** is a closed plane figure made of straight line segments that meet at endpoints without crossing in the simple polygons studied here. A **[[vertex]]** is a corner where two sides meet. Coordinates can specify each vertex exactly, allowing another learner to reconstruct a shape without measuring a printed drawing. The order of the listed vertices tells how to connect them around the boundary.

For example, connect $A=(-2,1)$, $B=(4,1)$, $C=(4,5)$, and $D=(-2,5)$, then return to A. The result is a rectangle. Connecting them in a different order could create crossing segments, so a list of points alone is not always enough. State the boundary order or draw the intended connections.

## Read horizontal and vertical side lengths

Sides whose endpoints share a y-coordinate are horizontal. Their length is the separation of the x-coordinates. Sides whose endpoints share an x-coordinate are vertical, and their length is the separation of the y-coordinates. These are the axis-aligned distances learned earlier. Negative coordinates indicate location, not negative lengths.

For the rectangle above, AB runs from x equals negative two to x equals four, a length of 6 units. BC runs from y equals one to y equals five, a length of 4 units. The opposite sides match those lengths. The rectangle's position partly left of the y-axis does not reduce its area; the entire region still has positive width and height.

### Example 1: Find area and boundary length

Use the rectangle with vertices $(-2,1)$, $(4,1)$, $(4,5)$, and $(-2,5)$. Its width is $2+4=6$ units because it crosses the y-axis. Its height is $5-1=4$ units. The area is $6\times4=24$ square units.

The **[[perimeter]]** is the total length of a shape's boundary. Add all four sides: $6+4+6+4=20$ units. Alternatively use $2(6+4)=20$. The area and perimeter use different units and answer different questions, even though both come from the same coordinate measurements.

```plot
{"x":[-3,5],"y":[0,6],"equal":true,"polygons":[{"points":[[-2,1],[4,1],[4,5],[-2,5]]}],"points":[{"at":[-2,1],"label":"A"},{"at":[4,1],"label":"B"},{"at":[4,5],"label":"C"},{"at":[-2,5],"label":"D"}],"caption":"Rectangle ABCD spans x from negative two to four and y from one to five, giving width six and height four."}
```

Check by counting unit-square rows in a grid: four rows each contain six squares, giving 24. Then trace the boundary to confirm that perimeter counts every outside side exactly once. Interior grid lines are not part of the perimeter, even though they help count area.

## Decompose a more complex region

**[[Decomposition]]** splits a shape into simpler pieces whose areas can be calculated. The pieces must cover the original region exactly, with no gaps and no overlapping interiors. You can draw a horizontal or vertical line through a vertex to form rectangles, or draw a diagonal to form triangles. Choose a split that uses known or easily calculated dimensions.

An alternative is subtraction: enclose the shape in a larger rectangle and remove missing pieces. Both strategies can be correct. Comparing their results provides a strong check because the same region is measured in two different ways. Explain which edges are outside boundaries and which are temporary internal dividing lines.

### Example 2: Measure an L-shaped region

An L-shaped polygon has vertices $(0,0)$, $(6,0)$, $(6,2)$, $(2,2)$, $(2,5)$, and $(0,5)$ in that order. Split it into a bottom rectangle measuring 6 by 2 and an upper-left rectangle measuring 2 by 3. Their areas are 12 and 6 square units, so the total area is 18 square units.

Check by subtraction. The enclosing rectangle is 6 by 5, with area 30. The missing upper-right rectangle is 4 by 3, with area 12. Subtracting gives $30-12=18$. The two methods agree. For perimeter, trace the outside sides: their lengths are 6, 2, 4, 3, 2, and 5, totaling 22 units. The internal decomposition line is not added to the perimeter.

## Use a right triangle on a grid

A triangle with vertices $(-1,0)$, $(5,0)$, and $(-1,4)$ has a horizontal base of 6 units and a vertical height of 4 units. Since horizontal and vertical directions are perpendicular, these lengths can be used in $A=bh/2$. The area is $6\times4/2=12$ square units. You do not need the diagonal side length to calculate this area.

However, finding the triangle's perimeter would require all three side lengths, including the diagonal. Counting a horizontal-plus-vertical path between its endpoints would not give the diagonal length. This course's coordinate-distance work focuses on axis-aligned segments, so do not invent an unsupported diagonal measurement merely to complete a perimeter calculation.

## Apply a real scale

If each coordinate unit represents 2 meters, a 6-by-4-unit rectangle has physical dimensions 12 by 8 meters. Its area is $12\times8=96$ square meters, while its perimeter is $2(12+8)=40$ meters. Scaling each length by 2 scales area by 4, because area multiplies two dimensions. This is another reason to distinguish coordinate units from physical length and square units.

## Check that a decomposition is complete

After drawing a split, shade each piece in turn. Every point inside the original polygon should belong to one piece, apart from shared boundary lines that have no area. If a region remains unshaded, its area has been omitted. If two shaded interiors overlap, that overlap has been counted twice. This visual check is useful even when all individual rectangle calculations are correct.

## Common mistakes

Connecting vertices out of order can change the shape or cross its sides. Using a negative coordinate as a side length can produce an impossible negative area. Counting an internal decomposition edge as perimeter adds a boundary that is not exposed. Scaling area by a length factor only once ignores the second dimension. Sketch, label, and verify the shape before calculating.

## Key points

- Vertex coordinates and connection order define a polygon.
- Shared coordinates identify horizontal and vertical side lengths.
- Decompose or subtract simpler regions without gaps or overlap.
- Area measures covering; perimeter follows only the outside boundary.

lessons.title: Nets and surface area
lessons.body:
## Unfold a solid into a flat pattern

A **[[net]]** is a flat arrangement of faces that can fold along shared edges to form a solid without gaps or overlapping faces. A **[[face]]** is a flat surface of a polyhedron. Looking at a net helps you see every face, including surfaces hidden in a three-dimensional drawing. It also provides a practical model for the material needed to cover a closed box.

**[[Surface area]]** is the sum of the areas of all outside faces of a solid. It is measured in square units, just like the area of a flat shape. Surface area is not the amount a container holds; that is volume, studied next. Covering a box and filling a box ask different questions and require different measurements.

## Account for every face

A rectangular box with length $l$, width $w$, and height $h$ has six faces in three matching pairs. The top and bottom each have area $lw$. The front and back each have area $lh$. The left and right each have area $wh$. Adding all six gives $2lw+2lh+2wh$, or $2(lw+lh+wh)$.

The formula assumes a closed box with all six faces included. An open-top container omits the top face, so its material area is different. A task about painting only the side walls may omit both top and bottom. State which surfaces are included before applying a formula, and remember that real packaging may require extra material for seams or tabs beyond the ideal geometric model.

### Example 1: Cover a rectangular box

A closed rectangular box measures 4 centimeters by 3 centimeters by 2 centimeters. Its top and bottom are 4-by-3 rectangles, each with area 12 square centimeters. Its front and back are 4-by-2 rectangles, each with area 8. Its two ends are 3-by-2 rectangles, each with area 6. The total is $2(12)+2(8)+2(6)=24+16+12=52$ square centimeters.

```shape
{"polygons":[{"points":[[0,0],[4,0],[4,3],[0,3]]},{"points":[[0,3],[4,3],[4,5],[0,5]]},{"points":[[0,-2],[4,-2],[4,0],[0,0]]},{"points":[[-2,0],[0,0],[0,3],[-2,3]]},{"points":[[4,0],[6,0],[6,3],[4,3]]},{"points":[[0,5],[4,5],[4,8],[0,8]]}],"labels":[{"at":[2,1.5],"text":"4 × 3"},{"at":[2,4],"text":"4 × 2"},{"at":[2,6.5],"text":"4 × 3"}],"caption":"A six-rectangle net for a 4 by 3 by 2 box: two 4-by-3 faces, two 4-by-2 faces, and two 3-by-2 faces."}
```
