Check the count before the arithmetic: there are exactly six faces, grouped into three pairs. If you sum only 12, 8, and 6, you have counted one face from each pair and obtained half the surface area. If you multiply $4\times3\times2=24$, you have calculated volume instead of covering area.

## Check whether a net can fold

A valid net needs more than the correct total number of faces. Faces must connect along compatible edges and fold into the intended solid without overlap. For a cube, every face is a congruent square, but not every arrangement of six squares is a cube net. Imagining or physically folding a paper model helps identify whether two squares would try to occupy the same side.

A net's shared fold edges are not additional faces. Cutting a net into pieces does not create more surface to count in the ideal zero-thickness model. Label dimensions consistently across matching edges so that a 4-centimeter edge is not accidentally attached to a 3-centimeter edge in a proposed rectangular-box net.

## Include triangular faces

A **[[triangular prism]]** has two congruent parallel triangular faces joined by three rectangular side faces when it is a right prism. Each rectangle's one dimension matches a side of the triangle, and its other dimension is the prism's length. Surface area therefore includes both triangles and all three rectangles. A triangle's area uses its perpendicular height, not all three side lengths multiplied together.

### Example 2: Cover a right triangular prism

A right triangular prism has a right-triangle end with perpendicular legs 3 centimeters and 4 centimeters and hypotenuse 5 centimeters. Its length is 6 centimeters. Each triangular end has area $3\times4/2=6$ square centimeters, so both triangles contribute 12. The rectangular side faces have areas $3\times6=18$, $4\times6=24$, and $5\times6=30$.

Add all five faces: $12+18+24+30=84$ square centimeters. A second grouping uses the triangle's perimeter: $(3+4+5)\times6=72$ square centimeters for the three side rectangles, plus 12 for the ends. This agrees with 84. The 5-centimeter side matters for a rectangular face, even though it was not needed to find the right triangle's area.

## Trace the triangular-prism net

The three rectangles wrap around the prism. Their widths follow the triangle’s sides in the order 3, 5, and 4 centimeters, while every rectangle has the prism’s 6-centimeter length. Each triangular end attaches along a 3-centimeter edge. Trace its other edges: the 5-centimeter edge meets the 5-by-6 rectangle and the 4-centimeter edge meets the 4-by-6 rectangle when folded. Both congruent triangular ends close the prism.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [3, 0], [3, 6], [0, 6]]}, {"points": [[3, 0], [8, 0], [8, 6], [3, 6]]}, {"points": [[8, 0], [12, 0], [12, 6], [8, 6]]}, {"points": [[0, 0], [3, 0], [0, -4]]}, {"points": [[0, 6], [3, 6], [0, 10]]}], "labels": [{"at": [1.5, 3], "text": "3 × 6"}, {"at": [5.5, 3], "text": "5 × 6"}, {"at": [10, 3], "text": "4 × 6"}, {"at": [0.8, -1.2], "text": "6 cm²"}, {"at": [0.8, 7.2], "text": "6 cm²"}], "caption": "A net for the right triangular prism has a strip of rectangles 3 by 6, 5 by 6, and 4 by 6 centimeters. Congruent 3–4–5 right triangles, each of area six square centimeters, attach to opposite three-centimeter edges of the first rectangle."}
```

Sketch the net on paper and label all five face areas before adding. The rectangles contribute 18, 30, and 24 square centimeters, and the two triangles contribute 6 each. Their sum is still 84 square centimeters; unfolding changes the arrangement, not the area.

## Adjust a model to the requested surfaces

If the 4-by-3-by-2 box from the first example has no top, subtract one 4-by-3 face from 52 to get 40 square centimeters. If only its four side walls are covered, omit both top and bottom, leaving 28. These answers differ because the surface sets differ, not because the earlier arithmetic was wrong.

If a real craft project requires overlap, glue tabs, or cutting waste, the exact face-area sum is a geometric minimum under the stated idealization. Do not invent an extra percentage without instructions. Explain what the area includes and let the practical requirements determine any added allowance. Also convert all lengths to compatible units before calculating each face area.

## Compare equal-sized faces

For a cube with edge length 3 centimeters, all six faces are congruent 3-by-3 squares. One face has area 9 square centimeters, so the surface area is 54 square centimeters. The volume would be 27 cubic centimeters. Comparing these two results makes the difference between counting outside squares and filling inside cubes especially clear, even for a highly symmetric solid.

## Common mistakes

Counting only visible faces misses hidden surfaces. Multiplying three dimensions calculates volume rather than area. Adding edge lengths produces a length measure instead of a covering measure. Treating any collection of the right faces as a valid net ignores folding compatibility. Label faces, count them, calculate their areas, and then sum only those the task includes.

## Key points

- A net displays faces and their folding connections.
- Surface area adds every included face area in square units.
- Closed rectangular boxes have three pairs of matching rectangular faces.
- Right triangular prisms include two triangles and three rectangles.

lessons.title: Volume with fractional edge lengths
lessons.body:
## Measure space with equal cubes

**[[Volume]]** measures the three-dimensional space occupied by a solid or available inside a container. A **[[cubic unit]]** is the volume of a cube whose edges each measure one chosen length unit. A box filled by three cubes along its length, two along its width, and four layers high contains $3\times2\times4=24$ unit cubes. Its volume is 24 cubic units.

A **[[rectangular prism]]** has six rectangular faces arranged in three opposite pairs. For a right rectangular prism, the volume formula is $V=lwh$, where the three measurements are mutually perpendicular edge lengths. The formula counts cubes in one layer, $lw$, and then multiplies by the number of layers, $h$. With fractional edges, the same reasoning uses smaller equal cubes.

## Connect layers to the volume formula

A prism 4 centimeters long, 3 centimeters wide, and 2 centimeters high has a base area of $4\times3=12$ square centimeters. Each one-centimeter-high layer contains 12 cubic centimeters, and two layers contain 24. The alternative formula $V=Bh$ uses $B$ for the base area. Because $B=lw$, it is equivalent to $V=lwh$.

The capital B in this formula names an area, not an edge length. Its units are square centimeters; multiplying by height in centimeters gives cubic centimeters. This unit reasoning distinguishes volume from surface area, which adds face areas and remains in square units. A box can have a volume of 24 cubic centimeters and a different surface area, such as 52 square centimeters.

## Subdivide when edges are fractional

A **[[fractional unit cube]]** has an edge that is a unit fraction of the chosen length unit, such as one half or one third. A cube with half-unit edges has volume $(1/2)^3=1/8$ cubic unit. Eight such cubes fill one unit cube because two fit along each of its three dimensions. A cube with third-unit edges has volume $1/27$ cubic unit.

The smaller cube's volume is not equal to its edge length. Halving each edge changes three dimensions, so the volume becomes one eighth, not one half. This repeated-dimensional effect connects to the area conversion work, where halving both sides of a square makes its area one quarter as large.

### Example 1: Count half-unit cubes

A rectangular prism measures $3/2$ units by 1 unit by $1/2$ unit. Use cubes with edge $1/2$ unit. Along the length, $3/2\div1/2=3$ cubes fit. Along the width, $1\div1/2=2$ fit. Along the height, one fits. The prism therefore contains $3\times2\times1=6$ small cubes.

Each small cube has volume $1/8$ cubic unit, so the total volume is $6/8=3/4$ cubic unit. Check with the edge-product formula: $(3/2)\times1\times(1/2)=3/4$. The two methods agree. The count 6 refers to half-unit cubes, not whole cubic units; labeling that distinction prevents an eightfold overstatement of the volume.

| Direction | Prism edge | Small-cube edge | Number fitting |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length | $3/2$ | $1/2$ | 3 |
| Width | $1$ | $1/2$ | 2 |
| Height | $1/2$ | $1/2$ | 1 |

## Choose a common subdivision

If the edges use halves and thirds, sixth-unit cubes provide a common subdivision. For a prism of dimensions $1/2$, $2/3$, and 1 unit, there are 3, 4, and 6 sixth-unit cubes along the respective directions. Their count is 72. Each cube has volume $1/216$, so the prism's volume is $72/216=1/3$ cubic unit.

The direct product gives the same result: $(1/2)(2/3)(1)=1/3$. The cube model explains why multiplying fractional edges works rather than simply offering a rule to memorize. Choosing a common denominator lets each edge contain a whole number of the smaller cube edges, making the packing count exact.

### Example 2: Calculate and interpret a fractional volume

A rectangular container has inside dimensions 2.5 meters by 1.5 meters by 0.4 meter. Its volume is $2.5\times1.5\times0.4$. First multiply $2.5\times0.4=1$, then multiply by 1.5 to obtain 1.5 cubic meters. Regrouping multiplication makes the decimal calculation efficient without changing the result.

Using tenths of a meter as cube edges gives 25 cubes along the length, 15 along the width, and 4 along the height. The count is $25\times15\times4=1500$ small cubes. Each has volume $0.1^3=0.001$ cubic meter, so the total is $1500\times0.001=1.5$ cubic meters. The inside dimensions matter because outside measurements would include the container's wall thickness.

## Check scale and units

If all edge lengths double, volume grows by a factor of $2\times2\times2=8$. If only height doubles while the base stays fixed, volume doubles. State which dimensions change before predicting the effect. A phrase such as “twice as large” is ambiguous unless it identifies edge length, area, or volume.

Convert lengths to compatible units before multiplying. For example, 50 centimeters is 0.5 meter. A prism with edges 1 meter, 2 meters, and 50 centimeters has volume $1\times2\times0.5=1$ cubic meter. Multiplying the raw numbers 1, 2, and 50 and labeling the result cubic meters would mix scales and produce the wrong value.

## Distinguish capacity from a fill level

A container's full inside dimensions determine its capacity in this prism model. If it is only partly filled, use the current fill height with the same rectangular base area to find the contained volume. A container with base area 4 square meters and water depth 0.25 meter contains 1 cubic meter, even if its walls are taller. State whether height means the full container height or the current depth.

## Common mistakes

Adding edge lengths does not count filled space. Treating a half-unit cube as half a cubic unit ignores two dimensions. Reporting the number of small cubes without their volume confuses count with measurement. Using outside dimensions for inside capacity includes wall material. Verify with layers or a common cube subdivision, and attach cubic units to the final answer.

## Key points

- Volume counts space in cubic units.
- A rectangular prism has volume $lwh$ or base area times height.
- Fractional edge products agree with packing smaller equal cubes.
- Track the small cube's volume, compatible units, and the dimensions actually being measured.

lessons.title: Statistical questions and distributions
lessons.body:
## Ask a question that expects variation

“How many minutes did one named student read yesterday?” asks for a single fact. “How many minutes did students in this class read yesterday?” expects a collection of values that may differ. A **[[statistical question]]** anticipates variability in data and can be investigated by collecting and analyzing a set of observations. It identifies what will be measured and whose or which observations matter.

**[[Variability]]** means that values differ across observations. Different reading times, plant heights, or daily temperatures create variability. A statistical investigation does not treat this variation as an annoyance to erase. It describes the pattern and asks what the variation reveals. Even when some values repeat, the collection can still vary overall.

## Define an observation and its unit

An **[[observation]]** is one recorded value or response associated with a specified member, event, or measurement occasion. If you record one reading time for each student, each student contributes one observation. If you record the same student's reading time on ten days, each day contributes an observation. Those investigations answer different questions and should not be confused.

The unit and measurement rule belong in the question or data description. “Reading time in whole minutes during yesterday's independent-reading period” is more specific than “reading.” Decide how to record a day with no reading, how to handle missing responses, and whether values are rounded. A missing response is not automatically zero; zero asserts a measured absence of the activity.

## Describe a distribution

A **[[distribution]]** describes the values in a dataset and how often they occur. For the fictional reading times 5, 10, 10, 15, 15, 15, 20, and 30 minutes, the value 15 occurs three times, 10 occurs twice, and the other listed values occur once. A table or graph makes that pattern easier to see than an unordered list.

| Reading time in minutes | Frequency |
|---|---|
| 5 | 1 |
| 10 | 2 |
| 15 | 3 |
| 20 | 1 |
| 30 | 1 |

The frequencies add to eight, matching the number of observations. The distribution has a concentration around 10 to 20 minutes, a smallest value of 5, and a largest value of 30. The gap between 20 and 30 and the relatively high last value are features to notice, not reasons to delete a valid observation.

### Example 1: Improve an investigation question

A draft question asks, “Do students read enough?” This is unclear because “enough” has no stated criterion and the target group is unspecified. Rewrite it as, “How many minutes did each student in our class read independently yesterday?” The revised question identifies the group, measurement, and time period and anticipates different responses.

Collect one response per student under the same rule. Record zero when a student reports no independent reading, and mark an unanswered item as missing. Summarize only the responses actually obtained, and state how many are missing. If the class contains 20 students but only 16 respond, do not describe the data as complete for all 20 without qualification.

## Look for center, spread, and shape

A distribution's center describes a typical or balancing value, while spread describes how far observations vary. Shape describes features such as clusters, gaps, symmetry, or a longer tail on one side. Later lessons define numerical summaries, but you can begin with careful descriptions. For the eight fictional times, values cluster near 15 minutes, and the data extend from 5 to 30.

Two datasets can share a center while having different spread. The values 9, 10, and 11 are concentrated near 10. The values 0, 10, and 20 have the same middle value but are more spread out. Reporting only the middle would hide that difference. A useful summary therefore considers both a typical value and the variation around it.

### Example 2: Compare two small distributions

Two fictional groups each report four practice times. Group A reports 8, 9, 10, and 11 minutes. Group B reports 2, 9, 10, and 17 minutes. Both groups have the same total, 38 minutes, and the same two middle values, 9 and 10. Their centers will therefore agree under both mean and median calculations introduced later.

Their spreads differ. Group A extends from 8 to 11, a span of 3 minutes. Group B extends from 2 to 17, a span of 15 minutes. A statement that the groups practiced “the same amount” is ambiguous: their total and center match, but the individual experiences vary much more in Group B. Specify which feature is being compared.

## Collect data that answer the question

A question about every student in a school is not fully answered by responses from only members of one reading club. The club's interests may differ from those of other students. At this level, recognize the limitation and describe the observed group accurately. Do not turn a convenient small collection into a claim about everyone without a reason it represents the broader group.

Data can also come from repeated measurement. Measuring one plant's height each week studies change over time; measuring many plants on one day studies differences among plants. In both cases, record what each observation represents. The same numerical list can support different interpretations depending on the collection process and units.

## Write a cautious evidence statement

A useful statement might be, “Among these eight fictional responses, most recorded times were between 10 and 20 minutes, with one response at 30.” This describes exactly the available data. It does not claim that all students everywhere behave that way or that longer reading caused another outcome. Description and causal explanation require different evidence.

## Common mistakes

A question with one predetermined numerical answer may not anticipate variability. Omitting units makes values hard to interpret. Replacing missing responses with zero changes the data. Reporting only a typical value can hide major differences in spread. Finally, generalizing from a narrow group without explanation goes beyond what the observations establish.

## Key points

- Statistical questions anticipate variation across a defined set of observations.
- Record the measured quantity, unit, group, and collection rule.
- Describe distributions using center, spread, shape, and context.
- Limit conclusions to what the collection process and available data support.

lessons.title: Dot plots and histograms
lessons.body:
## Choose a display that preserves the needed detail

A numerical list can hide repeated values and gaps. A **[[dot plot]]** places one dot for each observation above its value on a number line, stacking dots when values repeat. It preserves individual values, making it useful for a small dataset. A **[[frequency]]** is the number of observations at a value or within a specified group.

A **[[histogram]]** groups numerical values into adjacent intervals and displays the frequency in each interval with a bar. It can summarize a larger collection clearly, but it does not preserve each exact value. An **[[interval bin]]** is one of those numerical groups, defined by its boundaries and a rule specifying which boundary values are included.

## Build a dot plot

Use the fictional completion times 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, and 7 minutes. Draw a number line with equal spacing for equal time intervals. Place one dot over 2, two stacked dots over 3, three over 4, one over 5, and one over 7. Count all dots: there must be eight, because the original list contains eight observations.

```plot
{"x":[1,8],"y":[0,4],"points":[{"at":[2,1]},{"at":[3,1]},{"at":[3,2]},{"at":[4,1]},{"at":[4,2]},{"at":[4,3]},{"at":[5,1]},{"at":[7,1]}],"xLabel":"Completion time (minutes)","yLabel":"Stack position","caption":"Eight dots show times 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, and 7 minutes; each dot represents one observation."}
```

The stack height at 4 is three, so 4 minutes is the most frequent observed time. There is no observation at 6, creating a gap between 5 and 7. The dot plot also shows that most values lie between 3 and 5. The vertical placement within a stack does not give another measured variable; it only keeps repeated observations visible.

### Example 1: Read and verify a dot plot

From the displayed times, count observations taking at most 4 minutes. Include the dot at 2, both dots at 3, and all three dots at 4. That gives $1+2+3=6$ observations. “At most” includes the endpoint 4. If the question instead asks for fewer than 4 minutes, count only the first three dots.

Six of the eight observations are at most 4 minutes, so the share is $6/8=3/4=75\%$. This connects a data display to the percent methods studied earlier. Check the denominator carefully: it is the number of observations, not the number of distinct times. There are five distinct time values but eight observations.

## Define bins before counting

For a histogram of the same times, use equal-width intervals from 0 up to 2, from 2 up to 4, from 4 up to 6, and from 6 up to 8. Include each left endpoint and exclude each right endpoint. In symbols, the bins are $0\leq t<2$, $2\leq t<4$, $4\leq t<6$, and $6\leq t<8$.

This boundary rule puts a value of 4 in the third bin, not the second. Without a clear rule, an observation on a boundary might be counted twice or not at all. The intervals should cover all recorded values, and each observation should enter exactly one bin. Here the first bin is empty, which is still useful information.

### Example 2: Construct a histogram

Count values in each bin. The interval from 0 up to 2 contains none. The interval from 2 up to 4 contains 2, 3, and 3, giving frequency 3. The interval from 4 up to 6 contains 4, 4, 4, and 5, giving frequency 4. The interval from 6 up to 8 contains only 7, giving frequency 1.

```plot
{"x":[0,8],"y":[0,5],"bars":[{"x":1,"width":2,"height":0},{"x":3,"width":2,"height":3},{"x":5,"width":2,"height":4},{"x":7,"width":2,"height":1}],"xLabel":"Completion time (minutes)","yLabel":"Frequency","caption":"Equal-width bins [0,2), [2,4), [4,6), and [6,8) have frequencies 0, 3, 4, and 1. Left boundaries are included; right boundaries are excluded."}
```

Add the bar frequencies: $0+3+4+1=8$, matching the dataset size. The tallest bar represents the interval from 4 up to 6 minutes, not an exact time of 5 minutes. Its horizontal center is used to draw the bar; it does not assert that all four observations occurred at that center.

## Understand what grouping hides

The dot plot reveals three observations exactly at 4 minutes. The histogram only reveals four observations somewhere from 4 up to 6. You cannot reconstruct the exact original values from those bar heights alone. Another dataset with values 4.5, 4.7, 5.1, and 5.8 in that bin would produce the same frequency there.

Changing bin width can change the visible shape. Wider bins combine more detail; narrower bins expose finer variation but may produce many sparse bars. For this introductory work, use equal-width bins so bar heights can be compared directly as frequencies. Unequal-width bins require additional care and are outside this lesson's display method.

## Label and interpret the axes

A histogram's horizontal axis is numerical, ordered by value, and its bars correspond to adjoining intervals. A category bar chart instead compares named categories whose order may be chosen differently. In both displays, read the vertical scale carefully. A bar reaching the second grid line might represent 2 observations or 20, depending on the labels.

When writing a conclusion, describe both the concentration and any spread or gaps the display supports. For example, “Most times fall between 2 and 6 minutes, with one at 7” is supported by the original data. Avoid claiming that the tallest bin proves a single exact typical time. The display's level of detail limits the precision of your statement.

## Common mistakes

Counting only distinct values understates the sample size. Putting a boundary observation into both neighboring bins overcounts. Reading a bar center as an exact measured value invents detail. Using unequal horizontal spacing for equal time differences distorts a dot plot. Check dot or frequency totals and label the quantity, unit, and bin rule.

## Key points

- Dot plots retain individual values and repeated observations.
- Histograms group numerical values into explicitly defined intervals.
- Every observation belongs to exactly one bin, and frequencies sum to the count.
- Grouping makes patterns visible while hiding some exact detail.

lessons.title: Center and variability
lessons.body:
## Summarize a distribution with care

A numerical summary is useful only if you know what it measures. The **[[mean]]** is the sum of the observations divided by their count. It can be interpreted as a fair-share or balancing value. The **[[median]]** is the middle value in an ordered dataset, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even. These are two different measures of center.

Measures of spread describe variation around or across the data. The **[[range]]** is maximum minus minimum, but it uses only the two extremes. The **[[interquartile range]]** measures the width of the middle half of the ordered data. The **[[mean absolute deviation]]** measures the average absolute distance of observations from the mean. Pairing a center with a spread gives a fuller description than reporting either alone.

## Find mean and median

Use the fictional practice times 2, 2, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8, and 8 minutes. Their sum is 40, and there are eight observations. The mean is $40/8=5$ minutes. Imagine sharing the total time equally among the eight observations; each would receive five minutes. The mean need not be an observed value, and here no individual value is exactly 5.

The data are already ordered. With eight values, the middle positions are fourth and fifth, holding 4 and 6. Their average is $(4+6)/2=5$, so the median is also 5 minutes. Do not select just one of those two positions. For an odd count, one central position would determine the median directly.

### Example 1: Calculate a fair share and a typical distance

For the eight times, calculate each absolute distance from the mean of 5: the distances are 3, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 3, and 3 minutes. Their sum is 16. Divide by eight to obtain a mean absolute deviation, often abbreviated MAD, of $16/8=2$ minutes.

The MAD says that observations are, on average, 2 minutes from the mean. It does not say every observation is exactly 2 minutes away; in this dataset the individual distances are either 1 or 3. Taking absolute values prevents distances on opposite sides from canceling. Using signed differences would give a total of zero here and would fail to describe the visible spread.

| Time | Frequency | Distance from mean 5 | Total distance contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 2 | 3 | 6 |
| 4 | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| 6 | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| 8 | 2 | 3 | 6 |

## Find quartiles using a stated convention

Quartiles divide ordered data into sections. In this course, find the median first, split into lower and upper halves, and find each half's median. For an odd number of observations, exclude the overall median from both halves. Different software can use other conventions, so state this method when comparing small-dataset quartiles.

The lower half of our eight times is 2, 2, 4, 4. Its median is $(2+4)/2=3$, called the first quartile, Q1. The upper half is 6, 6, 8, 8, with median $(6+8)/2=7$, called the third quartile, Q3. The interquartile range, or IQR, is $Q3-Q1=7-3=4$ minutes. It describes the span between those two quartile markers.

### Example 2: Build and read a box plot

A **[[five-number summary]]** lists minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum. For our dataset, these are 2, 3, 5, 7, and 8 minutes. Draw a box from 3 to 7, a median line at 5, and whiskers extending to 2 and 8. This lesson uses whiskers at the minimum and maximum; other box-plot conventions may mark unusual values separately.

```shape
{"polygons":[{"points":[[3,1],[7,1],[7,2],[3,2]]}],"segments":[{"from":[2,1.5],"to":[3,1.5]},{"from":[7,1.5],"to":[8,1.5]},{"from":[2,1.2],"to":[2,1.8]},{"from":[8,1.2],"to":[8,1.8]},{"from":[5,1],"to":[5,2]}],"labels":[{"at":[2,0.5],"text":"Min 2"},{"at":[3,2.5],"text":"Q1 3"},{"at":[5,0.5],"text":"Median 5"},{"at":[7,2.5],"text":"Q3 7"},{"at":[8,0.5],"text":"Max 8"}],"caption":"A box plot on a linear minute scale has minimum 2, first quartile 3, median 5, third quartile 7, and maximum 8. The box width is the IQR of four minutes."}
```

The box width is 4 minutes, equal to the IQR. The overall span is $8-2=6$ minutes, equal to the range. The vertical height of the box is just a drawing choice; it represents no measured quantity. A **[[box plot]]** summarizes location and spread but does not show every observation or every repeated value.

## Consider unusual values and shape

Replace one final 8 with 40. The new sum is 72, so the mean becomes 9 minutes. The middle positions remain 4 and 6, so the median stays 5. The large value pulls the mean upward because every value contributes directly to the sum. The median depends on ordered position and can remain stable when an extreme value changes.

For a strongly one-sided distribution or one with an unusually distant value, median and IQR may describe the central bulk more clearly. For a roughly balanced distribution without extreme values, mean and MAD can be useful. These are context-sensitive choices, not rules that permit hiding inconvenient observations. Show the distribution and explain why the chosen summaries answer the question.

## Common mistakes

Finding a median before ordering the data can select the wrong middle. Dividing a mean by the number of distinct values ignores repeats. Using signed deviations instead of absolute distances makes cancellation hide spread. Mixing quartile conventions can create apparent disagreements. Finally, treating a box plot as a record of every observation invents detail it does not contain.

## Key points

- Mean and median measure center in different ways.
- MAD averages absolute distances from the mean.
- IQR is Q3 minus Q1 under a stated quartile convention.
- Box plots show a five-number summary, while shape and context guide which summaries to emphasize.

lessons.title: Data investigation and cumulative application
lessons.body:
## Plan a question and a bounded conclusion

A classroom wants to describe how long a short puzzle takes under two different instruction formats. A **[[data investigation]]** links a statistical question, a collection plan, a display, calculations, and a conclusion that stays within the evidence. The goal is not to rush to a single average. It is to explain what was measured, how values vary, and which claims the measurements can support.

This lesson uses invented data for practice, not results from actual students. A **[[sample]]** is a group of observations studied from a broader target group or process. A **[[sample limitation]]** is a feature of the collection that restricts how far conclusions can be extended. Small convenience groups, missing responses, different conditions, and uncertain measurement can all matter.

## State the fictional setup

Suppose eight fictional learners use Format A and eight different fictional learners use Format B. Times are recorded in whole minutes under the same stated timing rule. The two groups were convenient classroom groups, not randomly assigned. The question is, “How do the recorded completion-time distributions compare for these two groups?” This wording asks for a description rather than proof that one format causes faster work.

Format A times are 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, and 8 minutes. Format B times are 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, and 9 minutes. Each group has eight recorded observations. Check for missing entries and impossible units before analyzing. In this invented dataset, every observation is present and all times are positive.

| Group | Ordered times in minutes | Count | Total time |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8 | 8 | 48 min |
| B | 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9 | 8 | 48 min |

## Display the variation

A dot plot would show Format A concentrated from 4 to 8 minutes, with repeated values at 5, 6, and 7. Format B extends from 3 to 9, with only 6 repeated. Both groups have two central observations at 6. A histogram could summarize them using the same interval boundaries, but using different bins for the groups would make visual comparison less direct.

A table of exact values is sufficient for all calculations here, and it provides an accessible alternative to a display. When creating your own graph, label minutes on the horizontal axis and use the same scale for both groups. A compressed axis for one group could make equal spreads appear different or different spreads appear equal.

### Example 1: Compare centers and spreads

Both totals are 48 minutes, so each mean is $48/8=6$ minutes. Each median is also 6 because the fourth and fifth values are both 6. The centers therefore agree under these two summaries. Their ranges differ: Format A has $8-4=4$ minutes, while Format B has $9-3=6$ minutes.

Using the median-of-halves convention, A's lower half 4, 5, 5, 6 has Q1 equal to 5, and its upper half 6, 7, 7, 8 has Q3 equal to 7. Its IQR is 2. B's lower half 3, 4, 5, 6 has Q1 equal to 4.5, and its upper half 6, 7, 8, 9 has Q3 equal to 7.5. Its IQR is 3. Format B is more spread out by both range and IQR.

The MADs give another comparison. A's distances from 6 sum to $2+1+1+0+0+1+1+2=8$, so its MAD is 1 minute. B's distances sum to $3+2+1+0+0+1+2+3=12$, so its MAD is 1.5 minutes. All three spread summaries agree on the direction of the difference in these data.

## Connect percentages and unit conversions

Five of eight learners in each fictional group finish in at most 6 minutes. The fraction is $5/8=0.625=62.5\%$. The boundary matters: “at most 6” includes both observations equal to 6. If the question said “less than 6,” each group would have only three qualifying observations, or 37.5 percent.

Six minutes equals $6\times60=360$ seconds. Converting every time from minutes to seconds multiplies each mean, median, range, IQR, and MAD by 60. It does not change the fraction finishing within a correspondingly converted threshold. This connects units and percent reasoning to data analysis without changing the underlying observations.

### Example 2: Plan a follow-up using an equation

A teacher has a 50-minute session and reserves 8 minutes for instructions and review. Let $p$ be the time available for puzzle work. The equation $p+8=50$ gives $p=42$ minutes. If an ideal planning model allocates 6 minutes per round, $6r=42$ gives $r=7$ rounds. This uses the observed mean as a planning input, not a guarantee for every learner.

The original data include times above 6 minutes, so seven rounds may be unrealistic if every learner must finish each one before the next begins. A **[[model assumption]]** is a condition taken as true when using a simplified representation. Here the assumption of exactly six minutes per round omits individual variation and transitions. State that limitation and adjust the practical plan if the goal requires everyone to finish.

## Write a conclusion that matches the evidence

A supported conclusion is: “In these fictional groups, mean and median completion times were both 6 minutes, while Format B had greater variability.” It is not supported to say that Format A is universally better or that either format caused the observed differences. The groups contained different learners and were not randomly assigned, so other differences could matter.

A follow-up investigation could use a clearer comparison plan, consistent timing, a broader set of learners, and documented missing responses. Those improvements would address particular limitations, but they would not remove every source of uncertainty. Explain what additional evidence would help rather than promising certainty from a larger table alone.

## Common mistakes

Equal means do not imply identical distributions. Counting only values strictly below a threshold when the question says “at most” gives the wrong percent. Treating a mean as every person's predicted time ignores spread. Finally, turning a descriptive comparison into a causal claim goes beyond the stated collection design.

## Key points

- Connect question, collection, display, summaries, and conclusion.
- Compare center and variability, keeping units and threshold wording explicit.
- Use earlier arithmetic and algebra skills while stating model assumptions.
- Limit conclusions to the observed data and acknowledge collection limitations.

questions.stem: A tray holds 7 round buttons and 5 square buttons. What is the ratio of round to square?
questions.explanation: Round comes first: 7 round to 5 square. The total 12 is not requested.

questions.stem: There are 9 blue flags and 6 white flags, with no other flags. What is blue to all flags?
questions.explanation: The whole is 9 + 6 = 15. Blue to all is 9:15.

questions.stem: A pattern uses 4 stars for every 3 circles. Which statement keeps that order?
choices: For every 3 stars, there are 4 circles.
There are 4 more stars than circles.
There are 3 stars in every group of 4 shapes.
For every 4 stars, there are 3 circles.
questions.explanation: The first number counts stars and the second counts circles. One basic group has 7 shapes.

questions.stem: A jar has 8 red beads and 2 green beads, and nothing else. What fraction of all beads is green?
questions.explanation: There are 10 beads altogether, and 2 are green. Use the total as the denominator.

questions.stem: A box holds 11 pencils and 4 pens. What is the ratio of pens to pencils?
questions.explanation: The words ask for pens first and pencils second, giving 4:11.

questions.stem: A design uses 2 triangles for every 5 squares. What can you conclude without knowing the number of repeated groups?
choices: The complete design has exactly 7 shapes.
The design has 3 more squares than triangles in total.
Triangles make up 2/5 of all shapes.
Each complete basic group contains 7 shapes.
questions.explanation: A basic group contains 2 + 5 = 7 shapes. The full design can contain several groups, so its total is unknown.

questions.stem: There are 6 apple trees and 10 pear trees, with no other trees. Which comparison uses 6:16?
questions.explanation: All trees total 6 + 10 = 16. Thus 6:16 compares apple trees with the whole.

questions.stem: A student says 3:8 means 3 out of 8 objects are red. What additional information is needed to justify that interpretation?
choices: The 8 must count only objects that are not red.
The first number must be larger than the second.
The 8 must count all objects, and the 3 must count red objects.
The two numbers must have a difference of 5.
questions.explanation: A part-of-whole statement requires the second quantity to be the whole. Without labels, 3:8 could be a part-to-part comparison.

questions.stem: A box has 4 black tiles and 9 white tiles only. In black-to-all form, the second number is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The whole is 4 + 9 = 13 tiles.

questions.stem: A group contains 8 cats and 3 dogs. In dogs-to-cats form, the first number is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Dogs come first in the requested order, and there are 3 dogs.

questions.stem: There are 2 gold tokens and 5 silver tokens only. Match each comparison with its ratio.
questions.explanation: The total is 7. Keep each comparison's stated order.

questions.stem: A bag has 3 red and 4 blue counters only. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: There are exactly 4 counters in the bag.
questions.explanation: There are 7 counters. Red-to-blue is 3:4 and red-to-all is 3:7; blue-to-all would be 4:7.

questions.stem: Which ratio is equivalent to 3:5?
questions.explanation: Multiply both 3 and 5 by 4 to get 12:20. The other pairs do not use a common factor.

questions.stem: A mixture uses 5 scoops of oats for every 2 scoops of seeds. How many seed scoops go with 20 oat scoops?
questions.explanation: 20 is 4 times 5, so multiply the seed amount by 4: 2 × 4 = 8.

questions.stem: Each row of a ratio table lists (red counters, blue counters). The rows are (4,6), (8,12), and (12,?). What completes an equivalent-ratio table?
questions.explanation: The first row is scaled by 3: 4 × 3 = 12 and 6 × 3 = 18.

questions.stem: A bag has a red-to-blue ratio of 2:3 and 40 counters total. How many are red?
questions.explanation: One group has 5 counters. 40 ÷ 5 = 8 groups, so red is 2 × 8 = 16. Blue is 24, and the total is 40.

questions.stem: A student changes 2:7 into 5:10 by adding 3 to both parts. Why is the new ratio not equivalent?
choices: Equivalent ratios must keep the original total.
A ratio cannot contain a two-digit number.
The smaller quantity must always be divided by 2.
The two quantities were not multiplied by the same factor.
questions.explanation: 2 becomes 5 by multiplying by 2.5, while 7 becomes 10 by a different factor. Equal additions do not preserve this ratio.

questions.stem: A table has cups on the horizontal axis and servings on the vertical axis. Which point represents 6 cups and 15 servings?
questions.explanation: An ordered pair lists the horizontal value first: cups = 6, servings = 15.

questions.stem: A mix has 12 scoops of one ingredient and 18 of another. Divide both amounts by 6. What ratio results?
questions.explanation: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3. Dividing both by the same factor preserves the relationship.

questions.stem: A strip design has dark-to-light ratio 4:3. Which pair can describe a complete design made of whole strips?
questions.explanation: Scale 4:3 by 4 to get 16:12. Every count is whole, and both quantities share the factor.

questions.stem: The ratio 4:7 is scaled by 3. The second quantity becomes ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Multiply both quantities by 3: 4:7 becomes 12:21.

questions.stem: Red to blue is 3:2 and there are 25 counters total. There are ___ blue counters. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: One group has 5 counters, so 25 ÷ 5 = 5 groups. Each group has 2 blue counters: 5 × 2 = 10.

questions.stem: Match each multiplier applied to 2:5 with its resulting ratio.
questions.explanation: Apply the same multiplier to both entries in each pair.

questions.stem: Which ratios are equivalent to 4:6? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Divide by 2, multiply by 2, or multiply by 3 to obtain 2:3, 8:12, or 12:18. Adding 2 to make 6:8 changes the ratio.

questions.stem: Six identical folders cost 15 dollars. What is the price per folder?
questions.explanation: Divide dollars by folders: 15 ÷ 6 = 2.50. Multiplying by 6 recovers the 15-dollar total.

questions.stem: A cart travels 36 meters in 9 seconds at constant speed. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: Meters per second means 36 ÷ 9 = 4 meters for each second.

questions.stem: A machine makes 8 labels per minute at a constant rate. How many labels does it make in 7 minutes?
questions.explanation: Multiply the unit rate by time: 8 × 7 = 56 labels.

questions.stem: A printer makes 12 pages per minute at a constant rate. How long does it need for 48 pages?
questions.explanation: Divide target pages by pages per minute: 48 ÷ 12 = 4 minutes. Check: 12 × 4 = 48.

questions.stem: Three equal pieces of cord have a total length of 5 meters. What is the exact length of each?
questions.explanation: Meters per piece is 5 ÷ 3 = 5/3. The exact fraction avoids rounding. Three pieces total 5 meters.

questions.stem: A toy travels 18 meters in 6 seconds at constant speed. Which calculation gives seconds per meter?
questions.explanation: Seconds per meter places seconds first: 6 ÷ 18 = 1/3 second per meter.

questions.stem: A rover covers 21 meters in 6 seconds at constant speed. How far does it travel in 4 seconds at that speed?
questions.explanation: The rate is 21 ÷ 6 = 3.5 meters per second. Multiply by 4 to get 14 meters.

questions.stem: A cyclist averages 12 kilometers per hour on one trip. Which extra condition justifies predicting exactly 24 kilometers during a later 2-hour ride?
choices: The later ride uses the same bicycle.
The later ride starts at the same location.
The later ride happens on the same day.
The later ride maintains a constant speed of 12 kilometers per hour.
questions.explanation: The prediction requires the stated rate over the later interval. The bicycle, start or day alone does not establish that rate.

questions.stem: Seven identical tickets cost 21 dollars. The price is ___ dollars per ticket. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: 21 ÷ 7 = 3 dollars per ticket.

questions.stem: A machine runs at 5 parts per minute for 9 minutes. It makes ___ parts. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: 5 × 9 = 45 parts at the constant stated rate.

questions.stem: Match each calculation with the units of its result.
questions.explanation: The first quantity supplies the numerator unit, and the divisor supplies the unit after per.

questions.stem: A cart travels 20 meters in 5 seconds at constant speed. Which statements follow? Select all that apply.
choices: Its speed is 4 meters per second.
It needs 4 seconds to travel 1 meter.
It travels 12 meters in 3 seconds at that speed.
questions.explanation: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 meters per second. In 3 seconds it covers 4 × 3 = 12 meters. One meter takes 1/4 second.

questions.stem: Pack A has 3 identical brushes for 9 dollars. Pack B has 5 of the same brushes for 10 dollars. Which has the lower price per brush?
choices: Pack B at 2 dollars per brush
Pack A at 3 dollars per brush
Pack A at 9 dollars per brush
questions.explanation: A costs 9 ÷ 3 = 3 dollars each. B costs 10 ÷ 5 = 2 dollars each. Lower cost per brush favors B.

questions.stem: Cart A travels 40 meters in 8 seconds; cart B travels 27 meters in 3 seconds. Both speeds are constant. Which is faster?
choices: Cart A at 5 meters per second
Cart A at 40 meters per second
Cart B at 9 meters per second
questions.explanation: A travels 40 ÷ 8 = 5 meters per second; B travels 27 ÷ 3 = 9. Compare rates, not distances alone.

questions.stem: A robot moves at 9 meters per minute. How long does it take to cover 63 meters at that constant speed?
questions.explanation: 63 ÷ 9 = 7 minutes. Multiplying 7 minutes by 9 meters per minute returns 63 meters.

questions.stem: One runner travels 400 meters and another travels 500 meters. Can you determine which has the higher average speed?
choices: Yes; the runner covering 500 meters is faster.
Yes; the runner covering 400 meters is faster.
Yes; both have the same speed.
No; the time for each distance is also needed.
questions.explanation: Speed depends on distance and time. Neither distance by itself determines the rate.

questions.stem: A bundle of 4 pens costs 6 dollars; a bundle of 8 identical pens costs 10 dollars. You need 4 pens, must buy whole bundles, and want the lowest checkout total. Which should you buy?
questions.explanation: Although the 8-pen bundle has a lower unit price, the smallest purchase meeting this need is the 6-dollar bundle.

questions.stem: Offer A sells 2 identical cards for 5 dollars. Offer B sells 6 of the same cards for 12 dollars. Compare the cost of 6 cards.
choices: A costs 5 dollars; B costs 12 dollars.
A costs 10 dollars; B costs 12 dollars.
A costs 15 dollars; B costs 36 dollars.
A costs 15 dollars; B costs 12 dollars.
questions.explanation: Three A packs contain 6 cards and cost 3 × 5 = 15 dollars. One B pack contains 6 and costs 12 dollars.

questions.stem: A delivery costs 4 dollars plus 2 dollars per kilometer. A 3-kilometer delivery costs 10 dollars. What is the cost for 6 kilometers?
questions.explanation: The starting fee is paid once: 4 + 2 × 6 = 16. Doubling the distance does not double the entire fee.

questions.stem: Store A charges 12 dollars for 8 identical pencils. Store B charges 10 dollars for 5 of the same pencils. How much lower is A's price per pencil?
questions.explanation: A is 12 ÷ 8 = 1.50 dollars each; B is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 dollars each. The difference is 0.50 dollar per pencil.

questions.stem: One offer costs 18 dollars for 6 identical items. Another costs 20 dollars for 5 of the same items. The difference in unit prices is ___ dollar per item. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The unit prices are 3 and 4 dollars per item. Their difference is 1.

questions.stem: A cutter makes 7 shapes per minute at a constant rate. Making 56 shapes takes ___ minutes. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: 56 ÷ 7 = 8 minutes; 8 × 7 verifies the 56-shape target.

questions.stem: Match each question with the quantity that answers it.
left: Which identical-item offer costs less for one item?
Which cart covers more distance each second?
How long for a fixed distance at a known constant speed, using compatible units?
questions.explanation: Choose the comparison and operation that match the requested quantity and units.

questions.stem: A costs 8 dollars for 4 identical items. B costs 9 dollars for 6 of the same items. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Two A packs cost more than one B pack.
A has the lower unit price.
questions.explanation: A: 8 ÷ 4 = 2. B: 9 ÷ 6 = 1.50. B has the lower unit price. Two A packs cost 16 dollars, more than 9; they also contain a different number of items.

questions.stem: Write 0.35 as a percent.
questions.explanation: 0.35 is 35 hundredths, so it is 35%.

questions.stem: Which decimal equals 8%?
What percent is three quarters?
questions.explanation: Multiply 3/4 by 25/25 to obtain 75/100.

questions.stem: Six of 24 students cycle. What percent cycle?
A reference length is 20 cm. A new length is 30 cm. What percent of the reference is the new length?
questions.explanation: 30/20 = 1.5 = 150%. The reference is 20 cm.

questions.stem: In “12 of 60 tickets are sold,” what amount represents 100%?
questions.explanation: All 60 available tickets form the reference whole.

questions.stem: A learner writes 0.7 = 7%. What corrects the error?
questions.explanation: Seven tenths equals seventy hundredths.

questions.stem: Which equal 50%? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: One half, five tenths, and fifty hundredths are equal.

questions.stem: Write 0.09 as a percent. Enter only the number before the percent sign: ___.
Match each percent to its decimal multiplier.
questions.explanation: Divide the percent number by 100.

questions.stem: Find 20% of 75.
Find 35% of 160.
questions.explanation: 30% is 48 and 5% is 8; add to get 56.

questions.stem: A 60-dollar item is reduced by 25%. What is its price after the reduction?
questions.explanation: The reduction is 15 dollars; 60 − 15 = 45.

questions.stem: Find 125% of 24 m.
A learner uses 15 × 80 to find 15% of 80. Which multiplier should replace 15?
Exactly 10% of a group of 23 students is requested as a whole-student count. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: 0.10 × 23 = 2.3, which is not a whole-student count.

questions.stem: If 40% of 90 tiles are red and all the others are white, how many are white?
questions.explanation: The remaining share is 60%; 0.60 × 90 = 54.

questions.stem: Which methods find 30% of 50? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: All three selected methods give 15; division by 30 does not.

questions.stem: Find 5% of 200. Enter the number: ___.
questions.explanation: 1% is 2; five copies give 10.

questions.stem: Match each requested part to its amount.
questions.explanation: Use one half, one tenth, and one quarter.

questions.stem: 18 is what percent of 60?
12 is 25% of what number?
A learner finished 27 of 90 tasks. What percent is finished?
Twenty meters is 40% of a route. How long is the route?
Sixty is 120% of a reference number. Find the reference.
questions.explanation: 60/1.2 = 50, smaller than 60 because the percent exceeds 100.

questions.stem: Which operation finds what percent 9 is of 45?
questions.explanation: The part-to-whole fraction is 9/45; convert it to a percent.

questions.stem: Eight is 20% of a whole. A learner calculates 8 × 0.2. Why is this wrong?
questions.explanation: The whole solves 0.2 × whole = 8, so divide 8 by 0.2.

questions.stem: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
21 is what percent of 70? Enter only the number: ___.
Match the question to the missing quantity.
questions.explanation: Identify which of the three linked quantities has not been supplied.

questions.stem: Using 1 m = 100 cm, convert 2.4 m to centimeters.
Using 1 kg = 1000 g, convert 750 g to kilograms.
Using 1 hour = 60 minutes, convert 2.5 hours to minutes.
Which length is greater: 1.7 m or 165 cm? Use 1 m = 100 cm.
Using 60 seconds per minute, convert 180 meters per minute to meters per second.
questions.explanation: 180 meters in 60 seconds gives 180/60 = 3 m/s.

questions.stem: A square is 1 m by 1 m. Using 1 m = 100 cm, what is its area in square centimeters?
questions.explanation: Each side is 100 cm, so the area is 100 × 100 = 10000 cm².

questions.stem: Using 1 foot = 12 inches, convert 30 inches to feet.
Using 1 L = 1000 mL and 1 hour = 60 min, select the true equalities. Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Use 1000 mL per L and 60 min per hour; decimal hours are not hundredths of an hour notation.

questions.stem: Using 100 cm = 1 m, convert 325 cm to meters. Enter the decimal value: ___.
Match each quantity to an equivalent measurement. Use 100 cm/m, 1000 g/kg, and 60 min/hour.
questions.explanation: Multiply each count of larger units by the number of smaller units per larger unit.

questions.stem: Compute 936 ÷ 24.
Compute 1236 ÷ 12.
questions.explanation: The tens place needs a zero; 12 × 103 = 1236.

questions.stem: What are the whole-number quotient and remainder for 947 ÷ 24?
A van holds at most 16 boxes. How many vans are needed for 130 boxes?
questions.explanation: Eight vans hold 128 boxes; the remaining two need a ninth.

questions.stem: How many complete 18-cm pieces can be cut from 200 cm of ribbon?
questions.explanation: 18 × 11 = 198, leaving 2 cm; that is not another complete piece.

questions.stem: Which is a valid remainder when dividing a whole number by 15?
questions.explanation: A remainder must be less than the positive divisor.

questions.stem: A calculation says 832 ÷ 32 = 26. Which multiplication checks it?
questions.explanation: Division reverses multiplication: divisor × quotient = dividend.

questions.stem: Which division statements are correct? Select all that apply.
Compute 756 ÷ 28. Enter the quotient: ___.
For 157 ÷ 12 = 13 remainder 1, match each role to its number.
Compute 4.75 + 2.6.
questions.explanation: Write 2.6 as 2.60 and align place values.

questions.stem: Compute 5.02 − 1.78.
questions.explanation: Regroup across the zero tenths; 3.24 + 1.78 = 5.02.

questions.stem: Compute 2.4 × 0.35.
Compute 7.56 ÷ 0.6.
questions.explanation: Scale both numbers by 10: 75.6 ÷ 6 = 12.6.

questions.stem: Which calculation has the same quotient as 0.48 ÷ 0.12?
questions.explanation: Multiply both dividend and divisor by 100.

questions.stem: Why is 6 × 0.4 less than 6?
choices: The multiplier represents less than one whole
The divisor is larger than one
questions.explanation: 0.4 is four tenths, so the product keeps four tenths of 6.

questions.stem: Compute 8.1 ÷ 3.
Which are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The last subtraction is 2.3; the other operations preserve place value.

questions.stem: Compute 0.9 + 0.27. Enter the decimal: ___.
Match the operation to its result.
questions.explanation: Addition combines amounts, multiplication scales, and division counts groups of 0.3.

questions.stem: Compute $3/4 \div 1/8$.
questions.explanation: 3/4 = 6/8, so six eighths fit.

questions.stem: Compute $2/3 \div 1/4$.
questions.explanation: Multiply 2/3 by 4/1 to obtain 8/3.

questions.stem: Compute $5/6 \div 2/3$.
What is the reciprocal of 7/5?
A 5/6-m strip is cut into complete 2/3-m pieces. How many complete pieces can be made?
questions.explanation: The exact quotient is 5/4, but only one whole piece fits.

questions.stem: A learner flips both fractions when computing 2/5 ÷ 3/4. Which product is correct?
questions.explanation: Keep the dividend and multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor.

questions.stem: How many 3/4-kg portions are in 2 1/2 kg, counting fractional portions?
Which equal $1/2 \div 1/4$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Two quarter-size groups fit in one half.

questions.stem: Compute $7/8 \div 1/8$. Enter the number: ___.
questions.explanation: Seven eighths contains seven groups of one eighth.

questions.stem: Match the division to its quotient.
questions.explanation: Each quotient counts groups of one half.

questions.stem: Find the greatest common factor of 36 and 48.
questions.explanation: 12 divides both numbers; larger listed candidates do not.

questions.stem: Find the least common multiple of 6 and 8.
questions.explanation: The first shared positive multiple is 24.

questions.stem: Which number is a factor of 45?
Which is a multiple of 7?
questions.explanation: 42 = 7 × 6 with a whole-number multiplier.

questions.stem: Eighteen pens and 30 cards make the greatest possible number of identical kits with no leftovers. How many kits?
questions.explanation: The kit count is the greatest common factor of 18 and 30, which is 6.

questions.stem: Two signals repeat every 4 and 10 minutes, starting together. When do they next coincide?
questions.explanation: The least positive common multiple is 20.

questions.stem: Which uses the greatest common factor to rewrite 24 + 36?
questions.explanation: 12 is the greatest common factor; divide both terms by 12.

questions.stem: Which are common factors of 24 and 40? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 1, 4, and 8 divide both; 12 does not divide 40.

questions.stem: Find the least common multiple of 9 and 12: ___.
questions.explanation: 9 × 4 = 36 and 12 × 3 = 36; no smaller positive multiple is shared.

questions.stem: Match each request to its value.
questions.explanation: Check shared divisors for GCF and the first shared positive product for LCM.

questions.stem: Zero marks sea level. Which number represents 8 m below sea level?
questions.explanation: Below the zero reference is negative.

questions.stem: What is the opposite of −6?
questions.explanation: Opposites are equally far from zero on different sides.

questions.stem: Which statement about zero is correct?
choices: It is neither positive nor negative
questions.explanation: Zero is the reference separating positive and negative numbers.

questions.stem: Where is −1.5 on a number line?
questions.explanation: It is one and a half units left of zero.

questions.stem: East is positive. What does −4 km from a starting point mean?
questions.explanation: The sign gives direction; the distance is four kilometers.

questions.stem: What is the opposite of the opposite of −3?
questions.explanation: Two reversals return to the original number.

questions.stem: Which is a rational number?
questions.explanation: −3/4 is a ratio of integers with a nonzero denominator.

questions.stem: Which pairs are opposites? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Opposites have equal distance from zero; zero is its own opposite.

questions.stem: A change of −9 points is reversed. Enter the signed numerical change for the reversal: ___.
questions.explanation: Reversing a loss of nine points gives a gain of nine.

questions.stem: With ground floor at zero, match each position to its signed floor number.
questions.explanation: Above is positive, below is negative, and the reference is zero.

questions.stem: Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: −8 lies left of −3.
Absolute value is the distance from zero.

questions.stem: Which list is in ascending order?
questions.explanation: Move from left to right on the number line.

questions.stem: Which is greater, −3/4 or −2/3?
questions.explanation: They are −9/12 and −8/12; −8/12 lies farther right.

questions.stem: Which number has the greatest absolute value?
questions.explanation: Their distances from zero are 9, 2, 0, and 7.

questions.stem: Which is the greater signed balance: −12 or −5?
questions.explanation: −5 is greater even though −12 has the larger magnitude.

questions.stem: Which statement compares equal values?
questions.explanation: One half equals five tenths; both values have the same negative sign.

questions.stem: Which numbers are 6 units from zero? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Both opposites have absolute value 6.

questions.stem: Find $|-2.5|$. Enter the decimal value: ___.
questions.explanation: The point −2.5 is 2.5 units from zero.

questions.stem: Match each expression to its value.
questions.explanation: Absolute values give nonnegative distances from zero.

questions.stem: Where is (3, −2)?
questions.explanation: The first coordinate is horizontal; the second is vertical.

questions.stem: Which quadrant contains (−4, 2)?
questions.explanation: Negative x and positive y place the point upper left.

questions.stem: Which point lies on the y-axis?
questions.explanation: A zero x-coordinate places a point on the y-axis.

questions.stem: What are the origin’s coordinates?
questions.explanation: Both coordinates are zero where the axes meet.

questions.stem: A point is 2 units left and 5 units down. What is its ordered pair?
questions.explanation: Left makes x negative; down makes y negative.

questions.stem: Each grid interval is 0.5 km. A point is 4 intervals right and 3 up. Give its coordinates in kilometers.
questions.explanation: Multiply each interval count by 0.5.

questions.stem: Which describes (4, 0)?
questions.explanation: Its y-coordinate is zero, so it lies on the x-axis and in no quadrant.

questions.stem: Which points lie in Quadrant III? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Both coordinates must be negative.

questions.stem: For the point (−7, 4), enter the x-coordinate: ___.
questions.explanation: The first coordinate is x.

questions.stem: Match each sign pattern to its quadrant.
questions.explanation: Quadrants run counterclockwise from the upper right.

questions.stem: Find the distance from (−4, 2) to (3, 2).
questions.explanation: The horizontal segment crosses zero: 4 + 3 = 7.

questions.stem: Find the distance from (2, −3) to (2, 5).
questions.explanation: The vertical separation is 3 + 5 = 8.

questions.stem: Find the distance from (−6, 1) to (−2, 1).
questions.explanation: Both lie on the same side of zero, four units apart.

questions.stem: Reflect (3, 2) across the x-axis.
questions.explanation: The x-coordinate stays fixed and the y-coordinate changes sign.

questions.stem: Reflect (−4, 5) across the y-axis.
questions.explanation: The horizontal coordinate changes sign; y remains 5.

questions.stem: A horizontal map segment is 7 units long. Each unit is 10 m. What is its length?
questions.explanation: Multiply 7 coordinate units by 10 meters per unit.

questions.stem: A route goes from (−2, −1) to (3, −1), then to (3, 4). What is the route length?
questions.explanation: The horizontal and vertical segments are each 5 units; add their lengths.

questions.stem: Which pairs form axis-aligned segments? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: An axis-aligned pair shares x or shares y; the final pair shares neither.

questions.stem: Find the distance from (0, −7) to (0, 2). Enter the number of units: ___.
questions.explanation: Seven units to zero and two more gives nine.

questions.stem: Match the reflection of (2, −3) to its result.
questions.explanation: Reflection changes the coordinate perpendicular to the reflecting axis.

questions.stem: Evaluate $3^4$.
In $5^3$, what is the base?
questions.explanation: The base is the repeated factor, 5.

questions.stem: Evaluate $3+2^3\times4$.
Evaluate $24\div6\times2$.
questions.explanation: Division and multiplication share priority: 24/6 = 4, then 4 × 2 = 8.

questions.stem: Evaluate $(18-6)\div3+2^2$.
questions.explanation: Parentheses give 12; the power gives 4; 12/3 + 4 = 8.

questions.stem: Evaluate $30-12+5$.
questions.explanation: Subtract and add from left to right: 18 + 5 = 23.

questions.stem: Evaluate $7^0$.
questions.explanation: For a nonzero base, exponent zero gives 1.

questions.stem: Which equal 16? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The selected repeated products equal 16; 4 × 2 equals 8.

questions.stem: Evaluate $2+3^2$. Enter the number: ___.
questions.explanation: Evaluate 3² = 9, then add 2.

questions.stem: Match each expression to its value.
questions.explanation: Expand each exponent as repeated multiplication.

questions.stem: Write “five less than a number x.”
questions.explanation: Start with x and subtract five.

questions.stem: Write “three times the sum of x and two.”
questions.explanation: The whole sum x + 2 is multiplied by 3.

questions.stem: In 7n + 4, what is the coefficient of n?
questions.explanation: The numerical factor multiplying n is 7.

questions.stem: Evaluate 4k + 3 when k = 6.
Evaluate $2a^2+1$ when a = 3.
questions.explanation: The power applies to a: 2 × 9 + 1 = 19.

questions.stem: A rectangle has l = 7.5 cm and w = 4 cm. Evaluate A = lw.
questions.explanation: Multiply length and width: 7.5 × 4 = 30.

questions.stem: A group pays 4 dollars per kit plus one fixed 3-dollar charge. Which expression gives the cost of k kits?
questions.explanation: The per-kit cost is 4k; the fixed charge is added once.

questions.stem: Which expressions equal 11 when x = 3? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Substitution gives 11, 11, 11, and 15 respectively.

questions.stem: Evaluate 5n − 2 when n = 4. Enter the number: ___.
Match each phrase to its expression.
questions.explanation: Identify multiplication, addition, and division from the wording.

questions.stem: Expand 4(x + 3).
questions.explanation: Multiply each term inside by 4.

questions.stem: Simplify 3x + 2x + 7.
questions.explanation: Three copies and two copies of x make five copies; the constant remains 7.

questions.stem: Which is equivalent to 6x + 9?
questions.explanation: Distribution gives 6x + 9.

questions.stem: Which property changes 8 + x to x + 8?
questions.explanation: Only the order of the addends changes.

questions.stem: Which property changes (2 + x) + 5 to 2 + (x + 5)?
questions.explanation: The order is fixed while the grouping changes.

questions.stem: A learner says x + 2 and 2x are equivalent because both give 4 at x = 2. Which input disproves the claim?
choices: Only x = 2 is allowed in all expressions
questions.explanation: At x = 3 the values are 5 and 6.

questions.stem: Use distribution to find 7 × 19.
Which are equivalent to 5(x + 2)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Distribution gives 5x + 10, and addition permits rearrangement and regrouping.

questions.stem: In 6(y + 4) = 6y + ___, enter the missing constant.
Match each expression to an equivalent form.
questions.explanation: Distribute or combine matching variable terms.

questions.stem: Factor 12x + 18 using the greatest common numerical factor.
questions.explanation: The GCF of 12 and 18 is 6; divide both terms by 6.

questions.stem: Factor 8y + 12 using the greatest common numerical factor.
questions.explanation: The GCF is 4, leaving 2y and 3.

questions.stem: Evaluate 18 × 7 + 18 × 3 by factoring.
Which expanded form equals 5(x + 4)?
questions.explanation: Multiply both terms by 5.

questions.stem: Factor 6a + 9b + 12 using the greatest common numerical factor.
questions.explanation: Every coefficient is divisible by 3.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 15z − 10?
questions.explanation: Distribution returns 15z − 10.

questions.stem: Why is 6(2x + 18) not equivalent to 12x + 18?
questions.explanation: 6 × 18 = 108, so the expanded constant is wrong.

questions.stem: Which are equivalent to 10x + 15? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Expand each; the final expression has constant 75.

questions.stem: The greatest common numerical factor of 14x + 21 is ___.
questions.explanation: The greatest common factor of 14 and 21 is 7.

questions.stem: Match each expression to its factored form.
questions.explanation: Divide every term by the displayed common factor, then distribute to check.

questions.stem: What does the equals sign mean?
choices: Both sides have the same value
questions.explanation: Equality compares two values.

questions.stem: Which value solves x + 4 = 12?
Does n = 5 solve 3n = 15?
questions.explanation: Substitute into the multiplication on the left.

questions.stem: A student read 18 pages of a 50-page section. Which equation represents remaining pages r?
questions.explanation: Completed pages plus remaining pages equals the total.

questions.stem: Which is a true equality?
questions.explanation: Both sides equal 12.

questions.stem: Which value solves x + 0.25 = 1?
For which rational values of x is x + 0 = x true?
questions.explanation: Adding zero leaves every rational value unchanged.

questions.stem: Which equations are true when x = 4? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Substitution gives 9 = 9, 10 = 10, 12 = 12, and 8 = 9.

questions.stem: Test x = 3 in 2x + 1. Enter the left-side value: ___.
Match each equation to its solution.
questions.explanation: Substitute each candidate to make both sides equal.

questions.stem: Solve x + 7 = 19.
questions.explanation: Subtract 7 from both sides.

questions.stem: Solve 6x = 42.
questions.explanation: Divide both sides by 6.

questions.stem: Solve 0.4x = 6.
Solve (3/4)c = 9.
Solve x/5 = 3.2.
questions.explanation: Multiply both sides by 5.

questions.stem: Four equal groups must contain all 18 students, with whole students in each group. What does 4n = 18 show?
choices: No exact equal whole-student grouping exists
questions.explanation: The arithmetic result is 4.5, which is not a whole-student count.

questions.stem: Which pairs of equation and solution are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Substitute each value. The final pair gives 22, not 10.

questions.stem: Solve x − 4 = 9. Enter x: ___.
questions.explanation: Add 4 to both sides.

questions.stem: Match the equation to the operation that isolates x.
questions.explanation: Use the inverse of the operation applied to x.

questions.stem: Write “n is at most 30.”
questions.explanation: At most includes 30 and smaller values.

questions.stem: Write “r is longer than 2.5 meters.”
questions.explanation: Longer than excludes equality and includes larger values.

questions.stem: Which graph represents x > 4?
questions.explanation: Strict greater-than excludes 4 and includes points to its right.

questions.stem: Which value satisfies x < −2?
questions.explanation: −3 lies left of −2.

questions.stem: A workshop permits n ≤ 12 participants. Which value satisfies the full context?
questions.explanation: A participant count must be a nonnegative integer no greater than 12.

questions.stem: Which comparison includes its boundary value?
questions.explanation: The equality part of ≥ includes 7.

questions.stem: Over rational numbers, how many solutions does x > 4 have?
questions.explanation: There are infinitely many fractions and integers greater than 4.

questions.stem: Which values satisfy x ≥ 2.5? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Include the boundary and every larger value.

questions.stem: A closed endpoint at 6 with a rightward ray represents x ≥ ___.
questions.explanation: The boundary value shown is 6.

questions.stem: Match each phrase to its relation.
questions.explanation: At least means a minimum, at most means a maximum, and less than excludes equality.

questions.stem: In d = 3t, time t is chosen to calculate distance d. Which quantity is dependent?
questions.explanation: The output distance is determined from the input time.

questions.stem: For d = 3t, find d when t = 4.
Which point belongs to d = 3t when coordinates are (t, d)?
questions.explanation: At t = 2, d = 6.

questions.stem: A container starts with 5 L and gains 2 L per minute. Which equation models volume v after t minutes?
questions.explanation: The rate contributes 2t and the initial amount contributes 5.

questions.stem: In v = 2t + 5, what does 5 represent?
questions.explanation: At t = 0, the equation gives v = 5.

questions.stem: A table has t = 0, 1, 2, 3 and v = 5, 7, 9, 11. Predict v at t = 4 under the same rule.
questions.explanation: The output increases by 2 each minute; 11 + 2 = 13.

questions.stem: Why can elapsed time t not be −2 in this model?
choices: The dependent quantity must equal zero
Elapsed time is restricted to nonnegative inputs
questions.explanation: The context, rather than graphing in general, restricts the input.

questions.stem: Which pairs (t, d) satisfy d = 3t? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Multiply each input by 3; the final pair would require d = 9.

questions.stem: Under d = 3t, distance 15 corresponds to t = ___.
questions.explanation: Solve 3t = 15 by dividing by 3.

questions.stem: For v = 2t + 5, match each input to its output.
questions.explanation: Multiply t by 2, then add the initial 5.

questions.stem: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Find its area.
A parallelogram has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Find its area.
questions.explanation: Base times perpendicular height gives 40.

questions.stem: A trapezoid has parallel bases 6 m and 10 m and height 4 m. Find its area.
Which measurement is needed with a triangle’s base to find area?
questions.explanation: The height must meet the base line at a right angle.

questions.stem: A rectangle is 6 cm by 4 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: 6 × 4 = 24 square centimeters.

questions.stem: A triangle has base 3.5 cm and height 2 cm. Find its area.
A triangle has base 20 cm and height 0.5 m. Using 1 m = 100 cm, find area in square centimeters.
questions.explanation: Convert height to 50 cm; 20 × 50 ÷ 2 = 500.

questions.stem: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: A parallelogram has area base × perpendicular height
A triangle’s height is perpendicular to its base line
A triangle always has area base × height
questions.explanation: A triangle needs the factor one half; the other statements describe area correctly.

questions.stem: A triangle has base 12 units and height 3 units. Enter its area in square units: ___.
Match the shape description to its area formula.
left: Rectangle with sides l and w
Triangle with base b and height h
Trapezoid with parallel bases a and b and height h
questions.explanation: Each formula uses perpendicular dimensions and counts square units.

questions.stem: A rectangle has vertices (−2, 1), (4, 1), (4, 5), and (−2, 5). What is its horizontal side length?
questions.explanation: The distance from −2 to 4 is 6.

questions.stem: For the same rectangle, what is its area?
questions.explanation: Width 6 times height 4 equals 24.

questions.stem: For the same rectangle, what is its perimeter?
An L-shape is a 6-by-5 rectangle with a 4-by-3 corner removed. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Subtract the missing area: 30 − 12 = 18.

questions.stem: A right triangle has vertices (−1, 0), (5, 0), and (−1, 4). Find its area.
questions.explanation: Its perpendicular legs measure 6 and 4; halve their product.

questions.stem: Which line should be excluded when measuring the perimeter of a decomposed L-shape?
choices: An internal line dividing two pieces
questions.explanation: Perimeter follows the outside boundary, not internal divisions.

questions.stem: A 6-by-4-unit rectangle uses 2 meters per coordinate unit. What is its physical area?
questions.explanation: Physical dimensions are 12 m and 8 m, so area is 96 m².

questions.stem: Which pairs define horizontal or vertical sides? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The first three share one coordinate; the last is diagonal.

questions.stem: A rectangle spans x = −3 to x = 2 and y = −1 to y = 3. Enter its area in square units: ___.
questions.explanation: Width is 5 and height is 4, giving area 20.

questions.stem: Match each measurement to its description.
questions.explanation: These describe different features of a polygon.

questions.stem: Find the surface area of a closed 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm box.
How many faces does a closed rectangular box have?
questions.explanation: There are three pairs of opposite faces.

questions.stem: What does surface area measure?
choices: Total outside covering in square units
questions.explanation: Surface area sums face areas.

questions.stem: Remove the 4-by-3 top from the box with surface area 52 cm². What area remains?
questions.explanation: Subtract one top face of area 12.

questions.stem: A right triangular prism has triangle legs 3 and 4, third side 5, and length 6 cm. Find its surface area.
questions.explanation: Two triangle areas total 12; three rectangles total 72.

questions.stem: For that triangular prism, what is the area of the rectangular face along the 5-cm triangle side?
questions.explanation: The rectangle is 5 by 6.

questions.stem: Why might six equal squares fail to form a cube net?
choices: A cube needs eight square faces
Some arrangements fold with overlapping faces
questions.explanation: The arrangement must fold into six distinct faces without overlap.

questions.stem: Which face pairs belong to a closed 5-by-4-by-2 box? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Each pair comes from selecting two of the three dimensions.

questions.stem: A cube has six square faces of side length 3 cm. Enter its surface area in square centimeters: ___.
questions.explanation: Each face has area 9; six faces give 54.

questions.stem: Match each measurement to its role in the 4-by-3-by-2 closed box.
choices: Area of one top or bottom face
Area of one front or back face
questions.explanation: The three distinct face areas are 12, 8, and 6, each appearing twice.

questions.stem: Find the volume of a 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm rectangular prism.
What is the volume of a cube with edge 1/2 unit?
A prism is 3/2 units by 1 unit by 1/2 unit. Find its volume.
questions.explanation: Multiply all three edge lengths.

questions.stem: How many half-unit-edge cubes fill that 3/2 by 1 by 1/2 prism?
questions.explanation: There are 3 × 2 × 1 small cubes.

questions.stem: Find the volume of a 2.5 m by 1.5 m by 0.4 m prism.
questions.explanation: 2.5 × 0.4 = 1; multiply by 1.5.

questions.stem: If all three edge lengths double, what happens to volume?
questions.explanation: Each of three factors doubles: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

questions.stem: Using 100 cm = 1 m, find volume of a prism with edges 1 m, 2 m, and 50 cm in cubic meters.
questions.explanation: Convert 50 cm to 0.5 m, then multiply 1 × 2 × 0.5.

questions.stem: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: V = base area × height for a rectangular prism
Doubling only height multiplies volume by 8
A third-unit-edge cube has volume 1/27 cubic unit
questions.explanation: Doubling only one dimension doubles volume; the other statements follow from three-dimensional products.

questions.stem: A prism has base area 6 square units and height 1/2 unit. Enter volume in cubic units: ___.
Match cube edge length to cube volume.
questions.explanation: Multiply the edge length by itself three times.

questions.stem: Which question is statistical?
choices: How many minutes are in an hour?
What is the posted start time of one class?
How many minutes did each student in our class read yesterday?
questions.explanation: It anticipates different reading times across students.

questions.stem: What does variability describe?
questions.explanation: Variability means recorded values can differ.

questions.stem: A student leaves a reading-time response blank. How should it initially be recorded?
questions.explanation: Blank does not establish that the student read zero minutes.

questions.stem: For 5, 10, 10, 15, 15, 15, 20, 30, how often does 15 occur?
