questions.explanation: Count the three observations equal to 15.

questions.stem: For that dataset, how many observations are recorded?
questions.explanation: Count every value, including repeats.

questions.stem: Groups A = 8, 9, 10, 11 and B = 2, 9, 10, 17 have which difference?
questions.explanation: A spans 3 minutes; B spans 15. Both total 38.

questions.stem: Data come only from one reading club. Which conclusion is justified directly?
choices: Proof that reading causes higher scores
A complete description of the whole school
A claim about all students everywhere
A description of the responding club members
questions.explanation: The observed group is limited to the respondents.

questions.stem: Which details help define a reading-time investigation? Select all that apply.
choices: Replacing every missing response with zero
questions.explanation: Group, period, and unit define observations; replacing missing data invents values.

questions.stem: The list 4, 4, 6, 8, 8, 8 has ___ observations.
questions.explanation: Repeated values each count as an observation.

questions.stem: Match each feature to what it describes.
choices: Clusters, gaps, and the overall pattern
questions.explanation: A distribution summary should consider all three features in context.

questions.stem: For 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 7, how many dots are stacked at 4?
questions.explanation: The value 4 appears three times.

questions.stem: How many observations in that list are at most 4?
questions.explanation: Count 2, both 3s, and all three 4s.

questions.stem: Using left-inclusive, right-exclusive bins, where does the value 4 belong?
questions.explanation: Include the left endpoint of the third bin.

questions.stem: For that list, what is the frequency in 2 ≤ t < 4?
questions.explanation: The observations are 2, 3, and 3.

questions.stem: What does a histogram bar over 4 ≤ t < 6 with height 4 establish?
choices: The dataset contains only four observations
Four observations lie in that interval
questions.explanation: A grouped frequency does not give exact individual values.

questions.stem: What percent of the eight times are at most 4 minutes?
Which display retains each exact value in a small numerical dataset?
questions.explanation: Each dot appears at its observed value.

questions.stem: Which are necessary checks when building this histogram? Select all that apply.
choices: Every bin must have a nonzero height
questions.explanation: Empty bins are allowed; coverage, totals, and boundary rules are essential.

questions.stem: For 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 7, the bin 6 ≤ t < 8 has frequency ___.
questions.explanation: Only 7 lies in that interval.

questions.stem: Match each display feature to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Dot plots preserve values; histograms group them.

questions.stem: For 2, 2, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8, 8, find the mean.
questions.explanation: The sum is 40 and the count is 8; 40/8 = 5.

questions.stem: For the same ordered dataset, find the median.
questions.explanation: Average the fourth and fifth values: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.

questions.stem: Using medians of the lower and upper halves, find Q1 and Q3 for that dataset.
questions.explanation: The halves are 2,2,4,4 and 6,6,8,8; their medians are 3 and 7.

questions.stem: If Q1 = 3 and Q3 = 7, find the IQR.
questions.explanation: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 4.

questions.stem: The absolute distances from the mean are 3, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 3, 3. Find the MAD.
questions.explanation: Their sum is 16; divide by 8 to get 2.

questions.stem: In the original dataset, replace one 8 with 40. Which summary remains 5?
questions.explanation: The middle positions remain 4 and 6; the mean rises to 9.

questions.stem: What does the width of a box from Q1 to Q3 represent?
questions.explanation: The box spans Q3 − Q1.

questions.stem: Which values belong in a five-number summary? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The full five-number summary is minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.

questions.stem: Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 10, 12: ___.
questions.explanation: The ordered list has five entries, so the third is the median.

questions.stem: Match each summary to its calculation.
choices: Average absolute distance from the mean
questions.explanation: These summaries measure center or spread in distinct ways.

questions.stem: Format A has times 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8. What is its mean?
questions.explanation: The total is 48 and the count is 8; 48/8 = 6.

questions.stem: Format B has times 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9. What is its median?
questions.explanation: The fourth and fifth values are both 6.

questions.stem: Using medians of halves for Format B, what is its IQR?
questions.explanation: Q1 = 4.5 and Q3 = 7.5; subtract to get 3.

questions.stem: In Format A, what percent finished in at most 6 minutes?
questions.explanation: Five of eight qualify: 5/8 × 100 = 62.5%.

questions.stem: Convert the 6-minute mean to seconds using 60 seconds per minute.
questions.explanation: 6 × 60 = 360 seconds.

questions.stem: A 50-minute session reserves 8 minutes. Under a model of 6 minutes per round, how many rounds fit in the remaining time?
Which conclusion is supported by the fictional datasets?
choices: Their centers match, but Format B is more variable
Format A causes faster work for all learners
questions.explanation: Both centers are 6, while B has larger range, IQR, and MAD.

questions.stem: Which limitations apply to the stated comparison? Select all that apply.
choices: Different learners used the two formats
The groups were not randomly assigned
The data are fictional practice data
A matching mean proves identical experiences
questions.explanation: The design and fictional status limit claims; equal means do not establish identical experiences.

questions.stem: Format A’s absolute distances from mean 6 sum to 8 across eight observations. Enter its MAD: ___.
questions.explanation: 8/8 = 1 minute.

questions.stem: Match each summary for Format B to its value in minutes.
questions.explanation: Range is 9−3; IQR is 7.5−4.5; MAD is 12/8.

The pattern of data values and how often they occur.

The number of observations at a value or in a specified group.
A display of frequencies in adjoining numerical intervals.
A numerical interval used to group observations, with an explicit boundary-inclusion rule.
The sum of the observations divided by their count.
The middle ordered value, or the average of the two middle values for an even count.
The third quartile minus the first quartile, measuring the span of the middle half of ordered data.
The average of the absolute distances of observations from their mean.
A process connecting a statistical question, data collection, analysis, and an evidence-based conclusion.
A group of observations studied from a broader target group or process.
A feature of data collection that restricts the conclusions or generalizations supported.
A condition treated as true when applying a simplified representation.
A comparison of two quantities in a stated order.
A ratio comparing two groups within a collection.
A ratio comparing one part with the entire collection.
The amount in a part divided by the amount in the entire collection.
The entire quantity being discussed; nonoverlapping parts that exhaust it add to this quantity.
Ratios describing the same multiplicative relationship.
A number by which quantities are multiplied to scale a relationship. In these ratio tasks it is positive.
A labeled table of quantity pairs sharing the same ratio.
Two coordinates written in order: horizontal first and vertical second.
The coordinate point (0,0), where the horizontal and vertical axes meet.
A comparison of quantities with different units, such as meters and seconds.
A rate stated for one unit of the second quantity.
For each, or for every one.
A speed at which equal time intervals correspond to equal distances.
Prices stated per one item or one unit of a product.
The same amount used as a basis for comparing two offers or relationships.
An amount charged once, independent of the amount subsequently used in the model.
A value expressed without rounding, such as the fraction 2/3.
A named measure or count, such as meter, second or item.

cards.front: Red:blue is 2:5. What fraction is red?
cards.back: 2/7, because the whole basic group has 2 + 5 = 7 parts.

cards.front: Can a ratio determine the exact total?
cards.back: Not by itself. You also need a count, total or number of groups.

cards.front: How do you preserve a ratio while scaling?
cards.back: Multiply or divide both quantities by the same positive factor.
Adding the same amount usually changes the multiplicative relationship; 2:3 becomes 4:5 after adding 2.

cards.front: How do you split a two-part total?
cards.back: Add the ratio parts, divide the total by that sum, then multiply each part by the group count.
Total dollars divided by the item count.

cards.front: Can a unit rate be less than 1?
cards.back: Yes. Three dollars for four items is 0.75 dollar per item.

cards.front: When does rate times time predict distance?
cards.back: When the given speed applies over that time interval; these problems state constant speed.

cards.front: How do you compare different pack sizes?
cards.back: Compare matching unit prices or scale both to a common quantity.

cards.front: Does the lowest unit price always minimize checkout cost?
cards.back: No. Whole-pack purchase constraints and the quantity needed can change the lowest total payment.

cards.front: How do you find time from distance and constant speed?
cards.back: Divide distance by speed using compatible units; multiply back to check.

references.title: Unit rates and comparisons
references.body:
| Goal | Method | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Price per item | Cost divided by count | 18 dollars for 6 items gives 3 dollars each |
| Distance per time | Distance divided by time | 30 meters in 5 seconds gives 6 meters per second |
| Distance at constant speed | Speed times time | 6 meters per second for 8 seconds gives 48 meters |
| Time at constant speed | Distance divided by speed | 42 meters at 6 meters per second takes 7 seconds |

The units after “per” tell you the divisor. Rates may be fractions or decimals. An exact fraction such as $2/3$ avoids rounding error.

Compare the same units and quantities. Lower dollars per item is cheaper per item; higher meters per second is faster. A common quantity provides another check: compare what both offers cost for twelve items, for example.

Check assumptions: identical products, a constant rate, compatible units and any whole-pack restrictions stated in the problem. A starting fee plus a per-unit charge does not give a constant ratio of total cost to quantity. Missing time means distance alone cannot establish speed.

references.title: Ratio language and equivalent tables
references.body:
## Read the labels first

| Given 6 triangles and 9 circles only | Comparison |
|---|---|
| Triangles to circles | $6:9$ |
| Circles to triangles | $9:6$ |
| Triangles to all shapes | $6:15$ |
| Fraction of shapes that are triangles | $6/15=2/5$ |

Equivalent ratios multiply or divide both quantities by the same positive factor. For $6:9$, dividing both by three gives $2:3$. Adding three to both would give $9:12$, a different relationship.

## When a total is known

For a two-part ratio $2:3$ and total forty:

1. One group has $2+3=5$ parts.
2. There are $40\div5=8$ groups.
3. The parts are $2\times8=16$ and $3\times8=24$.
4. Check both the total ($16+24=40$) and the ratio ($16:24=2:3$).

For a coordinate graph, label the horizontal and vertical axes. A table row with first quantity four and second quantity six becomes $(4,6)$ when the axes follow that same order.

references.title: How to study Math 6
references.body:
## Before beginning

This unreleased draft contains all eight planned core modules of Math 6. Learner acceptance and release review are pending. Familiarity with multiplication, division, fractions and decimal place value will help. The separate manual readiness check can identify prerequisites to revisit; it does not automatically assign a grade level or diagnose a learning condition.

Use paper, counters or labeled sketches as helpful. No purchase, external account, microphone or personal information is needed. Read the explanation, attempt a worked example before uncovering its solution, then compare your method. Generated practice supplies fresh numerical inputs, and question reviews explain the assessed relationships.

## Build a repeatable study routine

1. State what each number measures or counts, including its unit and reference whole where relevant.
2. Sketch a model, table, number line or diagram when it clarifies the relationship.
3. Explain why your chosen operation fits before calculating.
4. Check with an estimate, inverse operation, substitution or second representation.
5. Use the lesson questions and module checkpoint to identify specific material to revisit.

A checkpoint samples the module's content; it is not proof of every aspect of mastery. Module checkpoints reuse selected lesson questions. Repeated practice should include explanations and new contexts, not only memorized answer positions.

## Complete a lesson and check your progress

Read the lesson, work the examples on paper, and use **Practice the math** for fresh numerical problems. The practice button opens the drills linked to that lesson. Its quick-reference buttons open the corresponding methods and definitions.

Choose **Take the quiz** when ready. The quiz panel states how many correct answers are needed to complete the lesson. A question left unanswered counts as incorrect. After an attempt, read the explanations for missed questions and return to the relevant example. **Retake the quiz** starts another attempt; an unsuccessful attempt does not mark an unfinished lesson complete.

After completing the fourth lesson in a module, use the module quiz offered on the result screen. It checks selected ideas across those four lessons. If you miss the required score, review the lessons and retake the module quiz. A passed checkpoint offers the first lesson in the next module; the last module returns to the lesson list.

The Progress page shows completed core lessons and passed module quizzes separately. Finishing the lessons can mark the course complete even while a module checkpoint remains to be passed. Continue using any unfinished checkpoints and missed-question explanations to guide review. Completion records, assessment scores and skill mastery describe different things; none replaces explaining a method and applying it to a new problem.

## Respond to mistakes

| If your mistake involves… | Revisit… |
|---|---|
| Reversed quantities, scaling or unit rates | Unit 1: Ratios and rates |
| Reference wholes, percent multipliers or incompatible units | Unit 2: Percents and measurement |
| Place value, remainders, fraction groups or factors | Unit 3: Number operations |
| Signed order, distance, coordinate order or reflections | Unit 4: Rational numbers |
| Operation order, substitution, distribution or factoring | Unit 5: Expressions |
| Equality, inverse operations, endpoints or input/output roles | Unit 6: Equations and relationships |
| Height, boundaries, faces, square units or cubic units | Unit 7: Geometry and measurement |
| Observation counts, bins, center, spread or sample limits | Unit 8: Statistical thinking |

An adult or peer can ask “What does each number represent?” and “How could you check that?” without supplying the answer. Explain a correction in your own words, then try a different example. A wrong attempt identifies something to practice rather than establishing a diagnosis.

## Transfer and cumulative work

Invent two offers for the same imaginary item. Give each a whole-number quantity and total cost. Compare unit prices, then introduce whole-pack restrictions and a percent reduction. Keep the original price and the remaining price distinct. Use fictional amounts; no shopping or spending information is required.

For geometry, sketch an original rectangular room on coordinates, state a scale, and calculate floor area and boundary length. Explain why those measurements use different units. For statistics, use the fictional datasets in the final lesson to compare center and variability, calculate a threshold percent, and state a limitation on the conclusion.

These written explanations are manual practice. They do not create an automatically scored mastery result or an instructional-hour certificate. Use the relevant quick-reference sheet while practicing, then attempt a similar task without it to check recall and reasoning.

references.title: Percents and measurement quick reference
references.body:
| Need | Method | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Decimal from percent | Divide percent number by 100 | $35\%=0.35$ |
| Part | Decimal multiplier × whole | $0.35\times80=28$ |
| Percent number | Part ÷ whole × 100 | $28/80\times100=35$ |
| Whole | Part ÷ decimal multiplier | $28/0.35=80$ |

Name the reference whole. Percent comparisons require a nonzero whole. A percent above 100 may compare an amount larger than its reference. For reductions, distinguish the removed amount from the remaining amount.

Use a stated unit equality. Multiply meters by 100 to get centimeters; divide centimeters by 100 to get meters. Rate conversions must account for both distance and time. Area and volume conversions repeat the length factor for each dimension. Always attach units and check by reversing the calculation.

references.title: Number operations quick reference
references.body:
- Whole-number division: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, with $0\leq r<d$ for positive divisor $d$. Interpret leftovers in context.
- Decimal addition and subtraction: align place values. Multiplication combines decimal scales. Division permits equal scaling of dividend and divisor.
- Fraction division: $(a/b)\div(c/d)=(a/b)(d/c)$ for nonzero divisors and valid denominators. A common-denominator model explains the result. Multiply back to check.
- Factors divide; multiples are built. GCF supports maximum identical groups; LCM supports earliest shared positive repeats.
- Distribution: $ab+ac=a(b+c)$. Extract the factor from every term.

references.title: Signed numbers and coordinates quick reference
references.body:
- Positive and negative signs describe direction from a stated reference. Zero is neither positive nor negative.
- Opposites have equal distance from zero. Absolute value is that nonnegative distance.
- Values increase to the right. For example, $-8<-3$ but $|-8|>|-3|$.
- Ordered pairs use $(x,y)$: horizontal first, vertical second. Quadrants I–IV have sign patterns $(+,+)$, $(-,+)$, $(-,-)$, $(+,-)$. Axis points belong to no quadrant.
- Equal y-coordinates give a horizontal segment; equal x-coordinates give a vertical segment. Distance is the absolute difference of the changing coordinate. Apply the map scale.
- Reflect across x-axis: $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$. Across y-axis: $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y)$.
- A horizontal-plus-vertical route length is not generally the direct diagonal distance.

references.title: Expressions quick reference
references.body:
- Positive whole-number exponents count repeated factors: $3^4=3\times3\times3\times3$.
- Evaluate groups, then powers, then multiplication/division left to right, then addition/subtraction left to right.
- Define variables, substitute consistently, and keep units. In $4x+3$, the coefficient is 4 and the constant term is 3.
- Equivalent expressions agree for all permitted inputs. A matching example does not prove equivalence; one counterexample disproves it.
- Distribution: $a(b+c)=ab+ac$. Factoring reverses it: $12x+18=6(2x+3)$.
- Combine matching variable terms: $3x+2x=5x$. A constant is not another coefficient of x.
- Addition and multiplication permit commutativity and associativity; subtraction and division do not generally permit them.

references.title: Equations, inequalities and relationships quick reference
references.body:
- Equality compares values. Test a solution by substituting it consistently into the original equation.
- Solve $x+p=q$ with $x=q-p$. Solve $px=q$ with $x=q/p$ when $p\ne0$. Apply the same valid operation to both sides.
- Strict inequalities $<$ and $>$ exclude the boundary; inclusive inequalities $\leq$ and $\geq$ include it. Open and closed endpoints communicate this difference.
- A solution set must respect context: people counts are nonnegative integers, while lengths can be fractional.
- Input is usually graphed horizontally and output vertically. Label quantities and units.
- A constant-rate model $d=3t$ starts at zero. A model $v=2t+5$ has rate 2 and initial output 5. Check tables by substitution and state the interval where the model is assumed to hold.

references.title: Geometry and measurement quick reference
references.body:
| Measurement | Formula | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Rectangle or parallelogram area | $bh$ | Square units |
| Triangle area | $bh/2$ | Square units |
| Trapezoid area, parallel bases a and b | $(a+b)h/2$ | Square units |
| Closed rectangular-prism surface area | $2(lw+lh+wh)$ | Square units |
| Rectangular-prism volume | $lwh=Bh$ | Cubic units |

Heights are perpendicular to their bases. For polygons on coordinates, use shared coordinates to find axis-aligned lengths. Decompose without overlap or subtract a missing region. Perimeter follows only the outside boundary.

A net must fold without overlapping faces; count all included faces. A right triangular prism has two triangular ends and three rectangular side faces. Open containers omit specified faces.

A cube of edge $1/n$ has volume $1/n^3$. Counting fractional-edge cubes and multiplying their volume explains fractional prism volume. Convert all lengths to compatible units first.

references.title: Statistics quick reference
references.body:
| Summary | Calculation or meaning |
|---|---|
| Mean | Sum ÷ observation count |
| Median | Middle ordered value, or average of the two middle values |
| Range | Maximum − minimum |
| Q1 and Q3 | Medians of lower and upper halves; omit the overall median from both halves for odd counts in this course |
| IQR | Q3 − Q1 |
| MAD | Average absolute distance from the mean |

Dot plots retain individual values. Histograms group values in explicit intervals; this course uses equal-width bins with left endpoints included and right endpoints excluded. Each observation belongs in exactly one bin.

A box plot summarizes minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum. The lesson convention uses minimum/maximum whiskers. Different software may use different quartile or whisker conventions.

Always report observation count, units, collection context, center, and spread. A missing value is not automatically zero. A mean is not every individual's value. Descriptive differences do not by themselves establish cause, and a narrow sample does not justify universal claims.

drills.title: Find the first ratio part
drills.prompt: There are {red} red and {blue} blue counters. In blue-to-red form, what is the first number? Give only the number.
drills.solution: Blue comes first in the requested order. The first number is **{blue}**.

drills.title: Find the whole
drills.prompt: A bag has only {red} red and {blue} blue counters. In red-to-all form, what is the second number? Give only the number.
drills.solution: Add both nonoverlapping parts: {red} + {blue} = **{whole}** counters altogether.

drills.title: Scale a ratio
drills.prompt: A pattern uses {first} squares for every {second} circles. How many circles go with {target} squares at that same ratio?
drills.solution: The square count is multiplied by {factor}. Multiply the circles by the same factor: {second} × {factor} = **{result}**.

drills.title: Reduce a pair to a target
drills.prompt: A mix uses {largeFirst} scoops of oats and {largeSecond} scoops of seeds. How many seed scoops go with {first} oat scoops at the same ratio?
drills.solution: Divide both amounts by {factor}. {largeSecond} ÷ {factor} = **{second}** seed scoops.

drills.title: Find a unit price
drills.prompt: {items} identical folders cost {cost} dollars. How many dollars does one folder cost at that price?
drills.solution: Divide total cost by count: {cost} ÷ {items} = **{price}** dollars per folder.

drills.title: Find a constant speed
drills.prompt: A cart travels {distance} kilometers in {hours} hours at constant speed. Give its speed in kilometers per hour as an exact fraction or whole number.
drills.solution: Divide distance by time: {distance} ÷ {hours} = **{speed:frac}** kilometers per hour. Multiply the rate by {hours} to recover {distance} kilometers.

drills.title: Compare unit prices
drills.prompt: Offer A has {aCount} identical items for {aCost} dollars. B has {bCount} of the same items for {bCost} dollars. How many dollars lower is A's price per item?
drills.solution: A is {aCost} ÷ {aCount} = {aRate} dollars each. B is {bCost} ÷ {bCount} = {bRate}. The difference is **{gap}** dollars per item.

drills.title: Find time from distance
drills.prompt: A robot moves at {speed} meters per minute at a constant speed. How many minutes does it need to cover {distance} meters?
drills.solution: Divide distance by speed: {distance} ÷ {speed} = **{minutes}** minutes. Multiplying back checks the distance.

drills.title: Percent to decimal
drills.prompt: Write {p}% as a decimal.
drills.solution: Divide by 100: **{result}**.

drills.title: Hundredths to percent
drills.prompt: {p} out of 100 tiles are blue. What percent are blue? Enter the number without a percent sign.
drills.solution: A rate of {p} per 100 is **{p}** percent.

drills.title: Find a percent part
drills.prompt: Find {p}% of {whole}.
drills.solution: Multiply {whole} by {p}/100. The part is **{result}**.

drills.title: Find the remaining count
drills.prompt: Of {whole} tiles, {p}% are blue and all others are white. How many are white?
drills.solution: Blue tiles: {p}/100 × {whole} = {part}. White tiles: {whole} − {part} = **{result}**.

drills.title: Find the percentage
drills.prompt: {part} of {whole} tiles are marked. What percent are marked? Enter the number without %.
drills.solution: {part}/{whole} × 100 = **{p}** percent.

drills.title: Reconstruct the whole
drills.prompt: {part} meters is {p}% of a path. How many meters long is the path?
drills.solution: Divide {part} by {p}/100. The whole is **{whole}** meters.

drills.title: Meters to centimeters
drills.prompt: Using 1 meter = 100 centimeters, convert {meters} meters to centimeters.
drills.solution: Multiply {meters} by 100: **{result}** centimeters.

drills.title: Convert meters per minute
drills.prompt: A cart travels {perMinute} meters per minute. Using 60 seconds per minute, find meters per second.
drills.solution: Divide {perMinute} by 60: **{speed}** meters per second.

drills.title: Divide by a two-digit number
drills.prompt: Compute {dividend} ÷ {divisor}.
drills.solution: The quotient is **{quotient}** because {divisor} × {quotient} = {dividend}.

drills.title: Find a remainder
drills.prompt: When {dividend} is divided by {divisor}, what is the remainder after making complete groups?
drills.solution: {divisor} × {quotient} uses {divisor} × {quotient} of the total. Subtract from {dividend} to leave **{remainder}**, less than {divisor}.

drills.title: Add and subtract hundredths
drills.prompt: Compute {a} + {b} and {a} − {b}. Enter the sum first and the difference second.
drills.solution: Align decimal places. The sum is **{result}**. Regroup if needed to subtract the smaller value from the larger; the difference is **{difference}**.

drills.title: Divide decimal quantities
drills.prompt: Compute {dividend} ÷ {divisor}.
drills.solution: Scale both by 10, then divide. Check {divisor} × {quotient} = {dividend}. Answer: **{quotient}**.

drills.title: Multiply decimal quantities
drills.prompt: Compute {a} × {b}. Give the exact decimal product.
drills.solution: Multiply the whole-number forms {aTenths} and {bHundredths}, then divide by 1000 for their combined scale. The product is **{result:dp3}** (trailing zeros may be omitted).

drills.title: Divide by a unit fraction
drills.prompt: Compute ({n}/{d}) ÷ (1/{groupDen}). Give an exact fraction or whole number.
drills.solution: Multiply {n}/{d} by {groupDen}/1. The quotient is **{result:frac}**.

drills.title: Divide two fractions
drills.prompt: Compute ({a}/{b}) ÷ ({c}/{d}). Give an exact fraction or whole number.
drills.solution: Keep {a}/{b} and multiply by {d}/{c}: **{result:frac}**.

drills.title: Greatest common factor
drills.prompt: Find the greatest common factor of {a} and {b}.
drills.solution: Compare the positive factors. The greatest factor shared by {a} and {b} is **{result}**.

drills.title: Least common multiple
drills.prompt: Find the least common multiple of {a} and {b}.
drills.solution: List positive multiples until the first shared value. That value is **{result}**.

drills.title: Find an opposite
drills.prompt: What is the opposite of {n}?
drills.solution: Reflect {n} across zero. The opposite is **{result}**.

drills.title: Reverse a negative position
drills.prompt: What is the opposite of {negative}?
drills.solution: The opposite lies {n} units right of zero: **{n}**.

drills.title: Distance from zero
drills.prompt: Find the absolute value of {n}.
drills.solution: Measure distance from zero: **{result}**.

drills.title: Greater of two negative numbers
drills.prompt: Which number is greater: {left} or {right}? Enter that number.
drills.solution: {right} lies farther right on the number line, so the greater value is **{right}**.

drills.title: Read a horizontal coordinate
drills.prompt: A point is ({x}, {y}). What is its x-coordinate?
drills.solution: The first entry is the horizontal coordinate: **{x}**.

drills.title: Read a scaled horizontal position
drills.prompt: A point is {steps} grid intervals left of the y-axis. Each interval is {scale} units. What is its x-coordinate?
drills.solution: Left is negative. Multiply −{steps} by {scale}: **{result}**.

drills.title: Horizontal distance across zero
drills.prompt: Find the distance in units from ({x1}, {y}) to ({right}, {y}).
drills.solution: The segment is horizontal and crosses zero. {left} + {right} = **{result}** units.

drills.title: Vertical distance
drills.prompt: Find the distance in units from ({x}, {a}) to ({x}, {b}).
drills.solution: Only y changes. The two y-coordinates are **{gap}** units apart.

drills.title: Evaluate a power
drills.prompt: Evaluate ${baseValue}^{exponentValue}$.
drills.solution: Use {baseValue} as a factor {exponentValue} times: **{result}**.

drills.title: Evaluate a mixed expression
drills.prompt: Evaluate {a} + {b}² × {c}.
drills.solution: First square: {b}² = {square}. Then multiply by {c}, then add {a}: **{result}**.

drills.title: Evaluate a variable expression
drills.prompt: Evaluate {a}x + {b} when x = {x}.
drills.solution: Substitute: {a} × {x} + {b} = **{result}**.

drills.title: Evaluate an expression with a square
drills.prompt: Evaluate {a}x² + {b} when x = {x}.
drills.solution: Square {x}, multiply by {a}, then add {b}. The value is **{result}**.

drills.title: Find a distributed constant
drills.prompt: Expand {a}(x + {b}). What constant follows {a}x + ?
drills.solution: Multiply the constant by {a}: {a} × {b} = **{result}**.

drills.title: Combine variable terms
drills.prompt: Rewrite {a}x + {b}x as one term. Enter the coefficient of x.
drills.solution: Add the numbers of copies: {a} + {b} = **{result}**.

drills.title: Find the common numerical factor
drills.prompt: What greatest positive whole-number factor can be taken from {a}x + {b}?
drills.solution: Find the GCF of {a} and {b}: **{result}**.

drills.title: Complete a factorization
drills.prompt: Complete {first}x + {second} = {factorValue}({a}x + ___). Enter the constant.
drills.solution: Divide the constant {second} by {factorValue}: **{b}**.

drills.title: Evaluate an equation side
drills.prompt: To test a candidate x = {x}, evaluate the left side {a}x + {b}. Enter its value.
drills.solution: Substitute consistently: {a} × {x} + {b} = **{result}**.

drills.title: Complete a true equality
drills.prompt: Complete {a} + ___ = {total}.
drills.solution: The missing amount is **{b}**, because {a} + {b} = {total}.

drills.title: Solve an addition equation
drills.prompt: Solve x + {p} = {q}.
drills.solution: Subtract {p} from both sides: x = **{x}**.

drills.title: Solve a multiplication equation
drills.prompt: Solve {p}x = {q}.
drills.solution: Divide both sides by {p}: x = **{x}**.

drills.title: First whole-number solution
drills.prompt: What is the least whole number satisfying x > {bound}?
drills.solution: Exclude {bound}; the next whole number is **{result}**.

drills.title: Largest whole-number solution
drills.prompt: What is the greatest whole number satisfying x ≤ {bound}?
drills.solution: The boundary is included, so the greatest value is **{bound}**.

drills.title: Find an output from a rate model
drills.prompt: A cart model is d = {rate}t, with d in meters and t in seconds. Find d at t = {time}.
drills.solution: Substitute the input: {rate} × {time} = **{result}** meters.

drills.title: Include the starting amount
drills.prompt: A volume model is v = {rate}t + {start} liters. Find v when t = {time} minutes.
drills.solution: Add the starting {start} to the increase {rate} × {time}: **{result}** liters.

drills.title: Triangle area
drills.prompt: A triangle has base {baseLength} cm and perpendicular height {height} cm. Find its area in square centimeters.
drills.solution: {baseLength} × {height} ÷ 2 = **{result}** square centimeters.

drills.title: Trapezoid area
drills.prompt: A trapezoid has parallel bases {a} m and {b} m and perpendicular height {h} m. Find its area in square meters.
drills.solution: Add parallel bases, multiply by height, then halve: ({a} + {b}) × {h} ÷ 2 = **{result}**.

drills.title: Rectangle area from coordinates
drills.prompt: A rectangle has x-coordinates {x1} and {right}, and y-coordinates 0 and {height}. Find its area in square units.
drills.solution: Width is {left} + {right} = {width}; height is {height}. Area is **{result}**.

drills.title: Rectangle perimeter from dimensions
drills.prompt: An axis-aligned rectangle spans {width} coordinate units horizontally and {height} vertically. Find its perimeter in units.

drills.title: Surface area of a closed box

drills.title: Surface area of a triangular prism

drills.title: Count observations from frequencies

drills.title: Describe a distribution span
drills.prompt: A dataset’s smallest value is {minimum} minutes and largest is {maximum} minutes. How many minutes separate them?

drills.title: Count stacked dots

drills.title: Combine interval frequencies

drills.title: Find mean absolute deviation
drills.prompt: Find the mean absolute deviation of {low}, {low}, {high}, {high}. The mean is {center}.

drills.title: Summarize an uneven distribution
drills.prompt: For the ordered times {v1}, {v2}, {v3}, {v4}, {v5}, {v6} minutes, find the mean, median, IQR, and MAD. Use medians of the lower and upper halves for quartiles. Enter exact fractions or whole numbers.

drills.title: Percent meeting a threshold
drills.prompt: In a fictional group of 8 learners, {qualify} meet a stated time threshold. What percent meet it? Enter only the number.

drills.prompt: A session lasts {total} minutes, with {reserve} reserved. If each round takes exactly {roundTime} minutes, how many rounds fit?
